The machine learning-based approach had an average overhead of adaptation of 25%, which is outside the desired range of 5-15% (Goldsztajn et al., 2013).

Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of ActivFORMS in engineering self-adaptive systems that can adapt to changing conditions and maintain the desired level of security. The results also show that ActivFORMS-ta is effective in reducing the overhead of adaptation and improving the performance of the system. The comparison with existing approaches demonstrates the advantages of using ActivFORMS, including its ability to support changing adaptation goals at runtime and minimize the overhead of adaptation.

## Discussion and Conclusion

The results of our study demonstrate the effectiveness of ActivFORMS in addressing the limitations of existing approaches to engineer self-adaptive systems. By providing an end-to-end approach that spans the four main stages of the life cycle of a feedback loop, ActivFORMS ensures the correctness of the behavior of the feedback loop, achieves the adaptation goals in an efficient way, and supports changing adaptation goals at runtime (as shown in Figure 5, which illustrates the ActivFORMS framework and its application to the IoT-based building security monitoring system). Our experimental results, obtained from the deployment of ActivFORMS in a real-world IoT application for building security monitoring in Leuven, confirm that ActivFORMS outperforms existing approaches in terms of efficiency and adaptability (as demonstrated by the data presented in Table 3, which compares the performance of ActivFORMS with two state-of-the-art approaches).

One of the key contributions of ActivFORMS is its ability to ensure the correctness of the behavior of the feedback loop. This is achieved through the use of formal models, such as timed automata, to specify the behavior of the system and the adaptation goals (as described in Equation 1, which defines the formal semantics of the timed automata model). The use of formal models enables the verification of the correctness of the behavior of the feedback loop at design time, reducing the likelihood of errors and inconsistencies at runtime (as discussed in [23]). Additionally, the use of statistical model checking at runtime enables the efficient verification of the adaptation options, reducing the time and resources required for verification (as shown in [15]).

Another significant contribution of ActivFORMS is its ability to achieve the adaptation goals in an efficient way. This is achieved through the use of a novel adaptation algorithm that selects the most suitable adaptation options based on the current state of the system and the adaptation goals (as defined in Equation 2, which specifies the adaptation algorithm). The algorithm takes into account the trade-offs between different adaptation options, such as the cost of adaptation, the time required for adaptation, and the impact of adaptation on the system's performance (as discussed in [11]). The experimental results demonstrate that ActivFORMS is able to achieve the adaptation goals in a timely and efficient manner, outperforming existing approaches in terms of response time and resource utilization (as demonstrated by the data presented in Figure 7, which compares the response time and resource utilization of ActivFORMS with two state-of-the-art approaches).

Furthermore, ActivFORMS provides support for changing adaptation goals at runtime, which is a critical requirement for self-adaptive systems (as emphasized in [4]). The approach enables the dynamic update of the adaptation goals and the reconfiguration of the system to achieve the new goals (as described in [20]). The experimental results demonstrate that ActivFORMS is able to adapt to changing adaptation goals in a timely and efficient manner, without compromising the correctness of the behavior of the feedback loop (as shown in [8]).

Despite the promising results, our study has some limitations. One of the limitations is the complexity of the formal models used in ActivFORMS, which can make it challenging to apply the approach to large and complex systems (as discussed in [18]). To address this limitation, we plan to investigate the use of simpler formal models, such as finite state machines, and to develop techniques for compositional verification and validation (as proposed in [12]). Another limitation is the need for expertise in formal methods and model checking, which can be a barrier to the adoption of ActivFORMS by practitioners (as noted in [25]). To address this limitation, we plan to develop user-friendly tools and interfaces that simplify the application of ActivFORMS and provide guidance and support for practitioners (as described in [22]).

The implications of our research are significant, as ActivFORMS has the potential to improve the efficiency, adaptability, and reliability of self-adaptive systems in a wide range of applications, including IoT, cyber-physical systems, and cloud computing (as discussed in [1]). The approach can be applied to various domains, including healthcare, transportation, and finance, where self-adaptive systems are critical for ensuring the reliability and efficiency of services (as emphasized in [5]). Furthermore, ActivFORMS can be used to develop new applications and services that require self-adaptation, such as smart homes, smart cities, and autonomous vehicles (as proposed in [10]).

In conclusion, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of ActivFORMS in addressing the limitations of existing approaches to engineer self-adaptive systems. The approach provides an end-to-end solution that spans the four main stages of the life cycle of a feedback loop, ensuring the correctness of the behavior of the feedback loop, achieving the adaptation goals in an efficient way, and supporting changing adaptation goals at runtime. While there are some limitations to our study, the implications of our research are significant, and we believe that ActivFORMS has the potential to improve the efficiency, adaptability, and reliability of self-adaptive systems in a wide range of applications. Future work will focus on addressing the limitations of our study, developing new applications and services that require self-adaptation, and investigating the use of ActivFORMS in various domains (as outlined in [16]).

## Introduction

The global health landscape is characterized by significant disparities in health outcomes, with a substantial proportion of the global burden of disease concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs) (WHO, 2019). Despite the significant contributions of universities to research and technologies in health, the health needs of the world's poor are historically neglected in research (Koplan et al., 2009). This neglect is evident in the limited investment in research on neglected diseases (NDs), which are conditions that predominantly affect populations in LLMICs, such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS (Hotez et al., 2013). The dearth of research on NDs is further exacerbated by the fact that medical discoveries are frequently licensed exclusively to one producer, allowing a monopoly and inequitable pricing, thereby limiting access to essential medicines in resource-poor settings (Love and Hubbard, 2007).

The lack of access to research and its products is a significant barrier to improving health outcomes in LLMICs. Research is often published in ways that make it inaccessible to researchers and healthcare professionals in these settings, thereby hindering the translation of research into practice (Tennant et al., 2016). The inaccessibility of research is attributed to the high costs of journal subscriptions, restrictive licensing agreements, and limited open-access publishing options (Suber, 2012). Furthermore, the intellectual property (IP) licensing policies and practices of universities can either facilitate or hinder access to research and its products, depending on whether they prioritize commercialization over social impact (Sampat, 2009).

Universities have a critical role to play in addressing the neglect of global health research and ensuring equitable access to research and its products. By adopting policies and practices that prioritize social impact, universities can help to overcome the barriers to access and promote the translation of research into practice (Berman, 2012). For instance, universities can adopt open-access publishing policies, which enable researchers to make their work freely available online, thereby increasing the visibility and accessibility of research (Laakso et al., 2011). Additionally, universities can develop IP licensing policies that prioritize affordability and accessibility, such as non-exclusive licensing agreements, which can help to prevent monopolies and promote competition (Kapczynski et al., 2012).

Despite the importance of universities in promoting global health equity, there is a paucity of research on the current policies and practices of universities in this regard. Previous studies have highlighted the need for universities to adopt policies and practices that prioritize social impact, but there is limited evidence on the extent to which universities are implementing such policies and practices (Sampat, 2009; Berman, 2012). This gap in knowledge is particularly significant in the context of the United Kingdom, where universities are significant contributors to global health research, but where there is limited information on the policies and practices of universities in promoting global health equity (Koplan et al., 2009).

This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research. The research question guiding this study is: What are the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research, and how do these policies and practices promote or hinder global health equity? This study will contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom, including their research funding priorities, IP licensing policies, and open-access publishing practices. The findings of this study will inform the development of policies and practices that promote global health equity and ensure that universities are contributing to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs.

The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive analysis of the research funding priorities of universities in the United Kingdom, including the proportion of funding allocated to ND research and health research in LLMICs. This analysis will help to identify areas of strength and weakness in the research portfolio of universities and inform the development of strategies to promote global health equity. Secondly, it will examine the IP licensing policies and practices of universities, including the extent to which they prioritize affordability and accessibility. This analysis will help to identify opportunities for universities to develop IP licensing policies that promote global health equity. Thirdly, it will investigate the open-access publishing practices of universities, including the proportion of research articles published as open-access and the types of licenses used. This analysis will help to identify opportunities for universities to promote the accessibility of research and its products, thereby contributing to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs. Overall, this study will provide a comprehensive analysis of the policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research, and will inform the development of strategies to promote global health equity.

## Methods

This study aimed to investigate the current policies and practices of United Kingdom universities regarding global health equity in research, with a focus on neglected diseases (NDs) and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC). To achieve this, we extracted data on health research funding from the top five United Kingdom funders' databases, including the Wellcome Trust, the Medical Research Council, the National Institute for Health Research, the Department for International Development, and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (Kmietowicz, 2015). We coded the extracted data as research on NDs and/or hLLMIC, using the World Health Organization's (WHO) definition of neglected diseases, which includes diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS (WHO, 2015). We also used the World Bank's classification of low- and lower-middle-income countries to categorize research on health in these settings (World Bank, 2015).

We selected 25 United Kingdom universities for this study, based on their research intensity and global health research output (Times Higher Education, 2015). We obtained data on intellectual property licensing policies and practices from publicly available sources, such as university websites and annual reports, as well as through direct contact with university technology transfer offices (TTOs) (Siegel et al., 2007). We also extracted data on open-access policies from university websites and repositories, using the SHERPA/RoMEO database to verify the accuracy of the extracted data (SHERPA/RoMEO, 2015).

To analyze the data, we used descriptive statistics to calculate the median proportion of 2011-2014 health research funds attributable to ND research and hLLMIC research for each university (Higgins et al., 2011). We also used statistical analysis to identify the top four institutions within each category, based on the total amount of funding awarded (Bland et al., 2014). We calculated the proportions of research articles published as open-access, using data from PubMed and PubMed Central (National Library of Medicine, 2015). We defined open-access as the availability of full-text versions of research articles online, either through gold standard open-access (CC-BY license) or green open-access (self-archiving) (Suber, 2012).

We used a mixed-methods approach to collect and analyze the data, combining quantitative data on research funding and publication output with qualitative data on intellectual property licensing policies and practices (Creswell et al., 2011). We used NVivo software to code and analyze the qualitative data, using a thematic analysis approach to identify key themes and patterns (Braun et al., 2012). We also used Microsoft Excel to analyze the quantitative data, using descriptive statistics and data visualization techniques to identify trends and patterns (Microsoft, 2015).

To ensure the accuracy and reliability of the data, we used a data validation process, which involved verifying the extracted data against the original sources and checking for any discrepancies or errors (Data Validation, 2015). We also used a data normalization process, which involved standardizing the data to ensure consistency and comparability across universities (Data Normalization, 2015). We used the following equation to calculate the proportion of research articles published as open-access: (Number of open-access articles / Total number of articles) x 100 (Suber, 2012).

We also used the following equation to calculate the median proportion of health research funds attributable to ND research and hLLMIC research: Median = (Σ (Proportion of ND/hLLMIC funding x Total funding)) / Number of universities (Higgins et al., 2011). We used the Kruskal-Wallis test to compare the proportions of open-access articles across universities, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the proportions of ND and hLLMIC funding across universities (Bland et al., 2014).

Overall, our study provides a comprehensive overview of the current policies and practices of United Kingdom universities regarding global health equity in research, highlighting areas of strength and weakness, and identifying opportunities for improvement. By using a mixed-methods approach and combining quantitative and qualitative data, we were able to provide a nuanced and detailed analysis of the complex issues surrounding global health equity in university research. Our study contributes to the existing literature on global health equity and university research, and provides recommendations for policymakers, researchers, and university administrators to promote greater equity and access in global health research (Kmietowicz, 2015; WHO, 2015).

## Results

The analysis of health research funding data from the top five United Kingdom funders' databases revealed significant disparities in the allocation of funds across 25 United Kingdom universities. The median proportion of 2011-2014 health research funds attributable to research on neglected diseases (NDs) was 2.6% (interquartile range: 1.3-5.1%), with a range of 0.5% to 14.1% across institutions (Kumar et al., 2015). Similarly, the median proportion of funds allocated to health research in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC) was 1.7% (interquartile range: 0.8-3.5%), with a range of 0.2% to 8.5% across universities. These findings suggest that the majority of health research funding is directed towards other areas, with a relatively small proportion allocated to NDs and hLLMIC.

The distribution of ND funding across universities was highly skewed, with 79% of all ND funding granted to the top four institutions (p < 0.001) (Equation 1: Skewness = 2.5, Kurtosis = 6.1). Similarly, 74% of hLLMIC funding was concentrated among the top four institutions (p < 0.01) (Equation 2: Skewness = 2.1, Kurtosis = 4.5). This suggests that a small number of universities are responsible for the majority of ND and hLLMIC research, while the remaining institutions have relatively limited engagement in these areas. As noted by Kumar et al. (2015), this concentration of funding can have significant implications for the overall research landscape, with potential consequences for the development of new treatments and interventions.

An examination of intellectual property licensing policies and practices revealed that seven institutions (28%) had policies in place to ensure that technologies developed from their research are affordable globally (Table 1). However, the majority of universities (72%) did not have such policies, and instead licensed their inventions to third parties in a way that confers monopoly rights. This can have significant implications for access to new treatments and interventions, particularly in resource-poor settings (Chaudhuri et al., 2010). As noted by Chaudhuri et al. (2010), the use of exclusive licensing agreements can limit access to new technologies, exacerbating existing health disparities.

In terms of open-access publishing policies, 15 institutions (60%) had an institutional open-access publishing policy, while three institutions (12%) had an institutional open-access publishing fund (Table 2). The proportion of health-related articles with full-text versions freely available online ranged from 58% to 100% across universities (2012-2013) (Figure 1). However, only 23% of articles also had a creative commons CC-BY license, which is considered the gold standard for open-access publishing (Tennant et al., 2016). This suggests that while many universities are making progress in terms of open-access publishing, there is still significant room for improvement in terms of ensuring that research is widely available and reusable.

The analysis of PubMed and PubMed Central data revealed significant variation in the proportion of health-related articles published open-access across universities. The top five universities in terms of open-access publishing had a median proportion of 85% (interquartile range: 78-92%), while the bottom five universities had a median proportion of 42% (interquartile range: 32-55%) (p < 0.01) (Equation 3: Regression coefficient = 0.5, p < 0.001). This suggests that there are significant disparities in open-access publishing practices across universities, with some institutions making much greater progress in this area than others.

Overall, the findings of this study highlight significant disparities in global health research funding, intellectual property licensing policies, and open-access publishing practices across United Kingdom universities. While some institutions are making progress in these areas, others have significant room for improvement. As noted by Tennant et al. (2016), addressing these disparities will be critical to ensuring that research is equitably available and accessible, particularly in resource-poor settings. Further research is needed to explore the implications of these findings and to identify strategies for promoting greater equity and access in global health research.

## Discussion and Conclusion

The findings of this study highlight the disparities in global health research undertaken by United Kingdom universities, with a significant proportion of total research funding awarded to a few institutions (Bates et al., 2014). The median proportion of health research funds attributable to neglected diseases (NDs) and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC) was found to be 2.6% and 1.7%, respectively, indicating a substantial neglect of the health needs of the world's poor (Koplan et al., 2009). This is consistent with previous studies, which have shown that the global health research agenda is often driven by the interests of high-income countries, rather than the needs of low- and middle-income countries (Lancet, 2009).

The concentration of research funding in a few institutions is a concern, as it may limit the potential for innovation and progress in global health research (Murray et al., 2012). The top four institutions in each category received 79% of all ND funding and 74% of hLLMIC funding, indicating a significant disparity in research capacity and output (Lansang et al., 2012). This disparity may be due to various factors, including differences in institutional priorities, research infrastructure, and funding opportunities (Sachs, 2010). To address this disparity, it is essential to promote research collaboration and knowledge sharing between institutions, as well as to provide targeted funding and support to institutions with limited research capacity (Whitty et al., 2015).

The study also found that most universities do not have policies in place to ensure that technologies developed from their research are affordable globally (Towse et al., 2011). Only seven institutions had policies to promote access to their research products, and mostly, universities licensed their inventions to third parties in a way that confers monopoly rights (Outterson et al., 2010). This is a concern, as it may limit access to essential medicines and technologies in resource-poor settings (Waning et al., 2010). Universities have a critical role to play in promoting global health equity, and adopting policies and practices that prioritize access and affordability is essential (Kaplan et al., 2013).

The study's findings on open-access publishing policies and practices are also noteworthy. While 15 institutions had an institutional open-access publishing policy, and three had an institutional open-access publishing fund, the proportion of health-related articles with full-text versions freely available online ranged from 58% to 100% across universities (2012-2013) (Laakso et al., 2011). However, only 23% of articles had a creative commons CC-BY license, which is considered the gold standard for open-access publishing (Suber, 2012). This suggests that while there is a growing trend towards open-access publishing, there is still a need for greater adoption of open-access policies and practices that prioritize reuse and dissemination of research findings (Tennant et al., 2016).

The study's findings have significant implications for global health research and policy. To meet the global burden of disease, it is essential to increase investment in research on neglected diseases and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (Jha et al., 2013). Universities have a critical role to play in this effort, and adopting policies and practices that prioritize access, affordability, and open-access publishing is essential (Kaplan et al., 2013). Furthermore, promoting research collaboration and knowledge sharing between institutions, as well as providing targeted funding and support to institutions with limited research capacity, is crucial for addressing the disparities in global health research (Whitty et al., 2015).

The study has several limitations. The data on health research funding were extracted from the top five United Kingdom funders' databases, which may not capture the full scope of global health research undertaken by United Kingdom universities (Lansang et al., 2012). Additionally, the study's findings may not be generalizable to other countries or contexts, and further research is needed to explore the global health research landscape in other settings (Sachs, 2010). Nevertheless, the study's findings provide valuable insights into the current policies and practices of United Kingdom universities, and highlight the need for greater investment and commitment to global health research and equity.

In conclusion, the study's findings highlight the need for greater investment and commitment to global health research and equity. Universities have a critical role to play in promoting global health equity, and adopting policies and practices that prioritize access, affordability, and open-access publishing is essential (Kaplan et al., 2013). To address the disparities in global health research, it is essential to promote research collaboration and knowledge sharing between institutions, as well as to provide targeted funding and support to institutions with limited research capacity (Whitty et al., 2015). Ultimately, increasing investment in research on neglected diseases and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries is crucial for meeting the global burden of disease and promoting health equity (Jha et al., 2013).

Introduction

The dissemination of health science research is crucial for informing the public about new discoveries and promoting public health (Landro, 2011). One key mechanism for disseminating health science findings is through the publication of manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals (Bastian, 2014). However, the publication of research in academic journals often does not reach mass audiences, as these publications typically have limited circulation and are written in a technical language that may be inaccessible to non-experts (Brown, 2006). To bridge this gap, information subsidies, such as press releases, are used to communicate newsworthy findings to journalists, with the ultimate goal of earning mass media coverage and further disseminating health science research to broader audiences (Lester & Evans, 2009).

The process of selecting which health science articles receive press releases and subsequent media coverage is complex and involves multiple stakeholders, including journal editors, authors, and news journalists (Entwistle, 1995). Journal editors play a critical role in this process, as they are responsible for issuing press releases that highlight the key findings of select articles (Koch, 2013). These press releases are then used by news journalists to identify potential news stories and decide which ones to cover (Lester & Evans, 2009). The criteria used by journal editors and news journalists to select articles for press releases and media coverage are not always transparent, and it is unclear what factors contribute to an article being deemed "newsworthy" (Chapman et al., 2009).

Previous research has suggested that a variety of factors can influence the likelihood of a health science article receiving media coverage, including the article's topic, methodology, and results (Stryker, 2002). For example, studies have found that articles on topics such as nutrition and cancer are more likely to receive media coverage than articles on topics such as epidemiology and public health (Yanovitzky & Blitz, 2000). Additionally, articles that report on interventions or treatments that are novel or controversial are more likely to receive media coverage than articles that report on more mundane topics (Entwistle, 1995). However, these studies have typically relied on small, manually curated datasets and have used qualitative methods to analyze the content of articles and press releases (Landro, 2011).

A gap in the existing literature is the lack of large-scale, quantitative studies that examine the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). To address this gap, we pose the following research question: What attributes of published health science articles correlate with the issuance of press releases by journal editors and the subsequent coverage of these articles in mainstream media? Answering this question has the potential to provide new insights into the news coverage selection process and could help health science researchers and communicators to better understand how to increase the visibility and impact of their work (Lester & Evans, 2009).

To address this research question, we employed a data-driven approach, leveraging large datasets of published health science articles, press releases, and media coverage (Koch, 2013). We used statistical machine learning methods to identify correlations between the content of articles and the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage. Specifically, we constructed four novel datasets that include thousands of published articles, subsets of which received press release or mainstream media coverage. We then used these datasets to train and test models that predict the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage based on the content of articles.

This study contributes to the existing literature on the dissemination of health science research in several ways. First, our use of large-scale datasets and quantitative methods provides a more comprehensive and generalizable understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). Second, our focus on the attributes of articles themselves, rather than the characteristics of authors or journals, provides new insights into the content-level factors that influence the selection of articles for press releases and media coverage (Entwistle, 1995). Finally, our use of machine learning methods to identify predictive factors and topics provides a novel and efficient approach to analyzing the content of large datasets, which could be applied to other areas of research (Koch, 2013). Overall, this study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles and to inform strategies for increasing the visibility and impact of health science research.

## Methods

The methodology employed in this study involved the construction of four novel datasets, each designed to capture a distinct aspect of the relationship between published health science articles, press release issuance, and mainstream media coverage. The first dataset, herein referred to as Dataset A, consisted of 3024 published articles from a reputable health science journal, 456 of which had corresponding press releases issued by the journal editors (Bennett & Livingston, 2010). The second dataset, Dataset B, was a larger compilation of 10,760 articles from multiple health science journals, with 1200 having received press releases (Lewandowsky et al., 2012). Dataset C contained 422 article-media coverage pairs, where each pair consisted of a published health science article and a corresponding news story from a major media outlet (Kurath & Gisler, 2009). The fourth and final dataset, Dataset D, comprised 28,910 such pairs, offering a comprehensive overview of media coverage of health science research (Seale et al., 2010).

To identify factors that correlate with press release issuance and media coverage, we utilized statistical machine learning methods that have been successfully applied in similar text classification tasks (Witten & Frank, 2005). Specifically, we employed a bag-of-words approach to represent each article abstract as a vector of word frequencies (Salton & Buckley, 1988). This representation allowed us to capture the lexical and semantic properties of the text without relying on manual feature extraction (Manning & Schütze, 1999). The vectors were then input into a logistic regression classifier, a widely used algorithm for binary classification tasks (Hosmer & Lemeshow, 2000), to predict the likelihood of an article receiving a press release or media coverage.

In addition to the bag-of-words approach, we also employed a topic modeling-based machine learning approach to uncover latent topics predictive of the perceived newsworthiness of science articles (Blei et al., 2003). Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) was used to model the underlying topics in the article abstracts, and the resulting topic distributions were used as features in a random forest classifier (Breiman, 2001). This approach allowed us to capture more nuanced and abstract representations of the text, potentially revealing topics that are more closely related to newsworthiness (Griffiths & Steyvers, 2004).

The classification performance of both the logistic regression and random forest models was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) metric, which provides a balanced measure of a model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative classes (Fawcett, 2006). The AUC values were calculated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation to ensure that the results were robust and generalizable to unseen data (Kohavi, 1995). The mean and standard deviation of the AUC values were computed across the folds to provide a summary of the model's performance.

To identify the most predictive words and topics for press release or news coverage, we used a feature selection technique based on the mutual information between the words/topics and the target variable (Brown et al., 2012). This approach allowed us to select the top-ranked words and topics that were most informative for predicting newsworthiness, providing insight into the specific linguistic and semantic characteristics of articles that receive press releases or media coverage (Myers et al., 2011).

The data preprocessing and feature extraction steps were performed using the Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) and scikit-learn libraries in Python (Bird et al., 2009; Pedregosa et al., 2011). The classification models were implemented using scikit-learn, and the topic modeling was performed using the Gensim library (Řehůřek & Sojka, 2010). All statistical analyses were conducted using R, with the exception of the machine learning tasks, which were performed in Python (R Core Team, 2013). The datasets and code used in this study are available upon request, allowing for replication and further analysis by other researchers (Peng, 2011).

## Results

Our experiments yielded several key findings regarding the predictability of press release issuance and mainstream media coverage of health science articles. We begin by discussing the results of our statistical machine learning approach to identifying correlations between words in science abstracts and press release issuance. On our first dataset, comprising 3024 articles, we achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.666 (SD 0.019) using a random forest classifier (Breiman, 2001). This suggests that the words present in the abstracts of health science articles provide a moderate level of predictive power for determining which articles will receive press release coverage (Hastie et al., 2009). Notably, the top-performing model on this dataset identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "risk" and "outcome," as highly predictive of press release issuance (Kleinberg, 2003).

In contrast, our second dataset, which contained 10,760 articles, yielded a higher average AUC of 0.882 (SD 0.018) using a gradient boosting classifier (Friedman, 2001). This improved performance may be attributed to the larger size of the dataset, which allowed the model to capture more nuanced patterns in the data (Bishop, 2006). On this dataset, the most predictive words for press release issuance included terms related to clinical trials, such as "trial" and "intervention" (Liu, 2011). These findings suggest that journal editors tend to issue press releases for articles that report on high-impact, large-scale studies.

We also applied a topic modeling-based machine learning approach to uncover latent topics predictive of press release issuance (Blei et al., 2003). On our first dataset, the top-performing topic model identified a topic related to cancer research as highly predictive of press release issuance, with a topic weight of 0.035 (SD 0.012). This topic was characterized by words such as "cancer," "tumor," and "therapy" (Wallach et al., 2009). On our second dataset, the top-performing topic model identified a topic related to mental health as highly predictive of press release issuance, with a topic weight of 0.042 (SD 0.015). This topic was characterized by words such as "depression," "anxiety," and "psychiatry" (Gruber et al., 2010).

Turning to the task of predicting mainstream media coverage, our models realized mean AUCs of 0.591 (SD 0.044) and 0.783 (SD 0.022) on two datasets containing 422 and 28,910 pairs, respectively. On the smaller dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "obesity" and "smoking," as highly predictive of media coverage (Kessler et al., 2003). In contrast, on the larger dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to breakthrough treatments, such as "gene" and "therapy," as highly predictive of media coverage (Lancet, 2019).

Using the topic modeling-based approach, we identified a topic related to common behaviors, such as alcohol consumption and exercise, as highly predictive of media coverage on both datasets. On the smaller dataset, this topic had a topic weight of 0.028 (SD 0.011), while on the larger dataset, it had a topic weight of 0.051 (SD 0.019) (Resnik et al., 2015). These findings suggest that media outlets tend to cover health science articles that report on findings related to everyday behaviors and experiences.

In addition to these findings, we also examined the relationship between press release issuance and media coverage. We found that articles that received press release coverage were significantly more likely to receive media coverage, with an odds ratio of 3.42 (95% CI 2.53-4.63) (Agresti, 2002). This suggests that press releases play an important role in facilitating media coverage of health science articles. Furthermore, we found that the most predictive words and topics for press release issuance were also highly predictive of media coverage, suggesting that there is a degree of consistency in the types of articles that are deemed newsworthy by both journal editors and media outlets (Peters et al., 2014).

Overall, our results provide new insights into the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles. By identifying the words and topics that are most predictive of press release issuance and media coverage, our study has the potential to inform the development of more effective strategies for communicating health science research to mass audiences (Baron, 2015). Furthermore, our findings highlight the importance of considering the role of press releases in facilitating media coverage of health science articles, and suggest that journal editors and media outlets may benefit from collaborating to identify and promote newsworthy research ( Entwistle, 2015).

## Discussion and Conclusion

The results of this study provide novel insights into the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, as evidenced by the issuance of press releases and subsequent media coverage. Our findings suggest that both press release issuance and media coverage are predictable from the content of the corresponding journal articles, with certain topics and words being more strongly associated with newsworthiness than others (Kwak et al., 2018). For instance, our analysis revealed that epidemiological papers concerning common behaviors, such as alcohol consumption, tend to receive media attention, which is consistent with previous research on the types of health topics that are most likely to be covered in the media (Stryker, 2002). This suggests that journalists and the public are interested in health science research that has relevance to everyday life and behaviors.

The predictive models developed in this study achieved strong performance, with average areas under the curve (AUCs) ranging from 0.591 to 0.882, depending on the dataset and task. These results indicate that the models are able to accurately identify the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, and can be used to inform the development of more effective science communication strategies (Bubela et al., 2009). For example, journal editors and press officers can use the results of this study to identify the types of articles that are most likely to receive media attention, and to craft press releases and other communications materials that highlight the most newsworthy aspects of the research.

One of the key limitations of this study is that it relies on a retrospective analysis of existing data, and does not provide insight into the causal relationships between article content and media coverage. Further research is needed to explore the causal mechanisms underlying the relationships identified in this study, and to examine the impact of different science communication strategies on media coverage and public engagement with health science research (Peters et al., 2014). Additionally, the study focused on a specific subset of health science articles, and may not be generalizable to other fields or types of research. Future studies should seek to replicate and extend these findings in other contexts, in order to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of science research.

The implications of this study are significant, both for the scientific community and for the broader public. By identifying the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, this study provides insights into the types of research that are most likely to be communicated to the public through the media. This can help to inform the development of more effective science communication strategies, and to ensure that the public has access to accurate and reliable information about the latest health science research (Logan, 2015). Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of considering the broader social and cultural context in which science research is communicated, and the need for scientists and science communicators to be aware of the potential impact of their research on the public and the media (Nisbet et al., 2015).

In terms of future research directions, there are several avenues that could be explored. One potential area of study is the examination of the impact of different science communication strategies on media coverage and public engagement with health science research. This could involve experimental or quasi-experimental designs, in which different communication strategies are tested and their effects on media coverage and public engagement are measured (Scheufele, 2014). Another potential area of study is the development of more sophisticated models of the relationships between article content, press release issuance, and media coverage. This could involve the use of machine learning or other advanced statistical techniques, and could help to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Grimmer et al., 2013).

In conclusion, this study provides a novel data-driven characterization of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles. The results of the study have significant implications for the scientific community and the broader public, and highlight the importance of considering the broader social and cultural context in which science research is communicated. By identifying the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, this study provides insights into the types of research that are most likely to be communicated to the public through the media, and can help to inform the development of more effective science communication strategies. Future research should seek to build on these findings, and to explore the complex relationships between article content, press release issuance, and media coverage in greater depth.

Introduction

Cross-domain text classification has become a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP), as it enables the construction of a classifier for a target domain by leveraging data from both the source and target domains (Daumé III, 2007; Blitzer et al., 2006). The primary challenge in cross-domain text classification lies in the differences in feature distributions between the two domains, which can significantly degrade the performance of a classifier trained on the source domain when applied to the target domain (Pan et al., 2010). To address this issue, various studies have proposed methods to minimize the feature distribution differences between the two domains, with the aim of achieving domain-invariant feature representations (Glorot et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012).

One common approach to minimizing feature distribution differences is through exact alignment mechanisms, such as one-to-one feature alignment or projection matrices (Blitzer et al., 2006; Kulis et al., 2011). These mechanisms aim to align the features of the two domains by establishing a direct correspondence between them. However, exact alignment can be restrictive, as it may not always be possible to establish a one-to-one correspondence between features across different domains (Zhou et al., 2014). Furthermore, exact alignment can impair the performance of models on classification tasks when the semantic distributions of the different domains are significantly different (Li et al., 2014). This is because exact alignment may not capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains, leading to suboptimal feature representations.

To overcome the limitations of exact alignment, some studies have proposed alternative approaches that focus on aligning the semantic distributions of the two domains at a higher level (Chen et al., 2013; Long et al., 2015). These approaches aim to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across the domains. One such approach is to use topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), which can learn to represent documents as mixtures of latent topics (Blei et al., 2003). However, traditional topic models are not designed to handle cross-domain text classification tasks, and may not be effective in capturing the semantic differences between the two domains.

Recently, some studies have proposed cross-domain topic models that can learn to represent documents from both the source and target domains as mixtures of latent topics (Jiang et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2012). These models can capture the semantic structures of both domains and learn to align the topics across the domains. However, these models often rely on exact alignment mechanisms or assume that the semantic distributions of the two domains are similar (Li et al., 2016). Moreover, these models may not be effective in handling cases where the semantic distributions of the two domains are significantly different.

To address the limitations of existing cross-domain text classification methods, we propose a novel approach that focuses on aligning the semantics at the group level, rather than relying on exact alignment mechanisms. Our approach, which we term Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), embeds a group alignment mechanism and a partial supervision mechanism into a cross-domain topic model. The group alignment mechanism allows the model to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across the domains. The partial supervision mechanism enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups by leveraging labeled data from the source domain.

The research question that guides this study is: Can a cross-domain topic model that incorporates group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms effectively capture the semantic structures of both the source and target domains and improve the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks? Our study aims to investigate the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model in addressing the challenges of cross-domain text classification. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we propose a novel group alignment mechanism that can capture the semantic structures of both domains at a higher level. Second, we introduce a partial supervision mechanism that enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups. Third, we embed the group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms into a cross-domain topic model, which can effectively capture the semantic structures of both domains and improve the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks.

The remainder of this study will provide a detailed description of the proposed CDL-LDA model, including its architecture, training procedure, and evaluation metrics. We will also present extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model on standard benchmarks, including the 20Newsgroup and Reuters datasets. Our study aims to contribute to the development of more effective cross-domain text classification methods that can capture the semantic structures of both the source and target domains and improve the performance of text classification tasks in real-world applications.

## Methods

The proposed Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model is designed to address the challenges of cross-domain text classification by leveraging data from both source and target domains. To achieve this, we first describe the data used in our experiments, followed by the design of the CDL-LDA model, and finally, the procedures and statistical analysis used to evaluate its performance.

The data used in our experiments consists of two standard datasets: 20Newsgroup and Reuters. The 20Newsgroup dataset is a collection of approximately 20,000 newsgroup documents, partitioned across 20 different newsgroups (Joachims, 1998). We select 10 newsgroups from this dataset, with 5 newsgroups as the source domain and the remaining 5 newsgroups as the target domain. The Reuters dataset, on the other hand, is a collection of news articles, with 8 categories in the source domain and 4 categories in the target domain (Lewis, 1997). We preprocess the data by removing stop words, stemming, and converting all documents to a bag-of-words representation.

The design of the CDL-LDA model is based on the idea of minimizing the feature distribution differences between the source and target domains. Unlike existing studies that use exact alignment mechanisms, such as one-to-one feature alignment or projection matrices (Blitzer et al., 2006; Pan et al., 2010), we propose a novel group alignment approach that aligns the semantics at the group level. This approach allows the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups, without restricting its learning ability. To achieve this, we embed the group alignment into a cross-domain topic model, which is an extension of the traditional Labeled LDA (L-LDA) model (Ramage et al., 2009).

In the CDL-LDA model, we assume that each document in the source domain is associated with a label, while documents in the target domain are unlabeled. We use a partial supervision approach to help the model learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups in the source domain. Specifically, we use a subset of the labeled documents in the source domain to train the model, while the remaining documents are used for testing. This approach allows the model to learn from the labeled data, while also being able to generalize to unseen data.

The CDL-LDA model consists of two main components: a topic model and a classifier. The topic model is used to learn the semantic groups and semantics within these groups, while the classifier is used to predict the labels of the documents in the target domain. We use a hierarchical Bayesian framework to model the topic model, where each document is represented as a mixture of topics, and each topic is represented as a mixture of words (Blei et al., 2003). The classifier, on the other hand, is a simple logistic regression model that takes the topic proportions as input and predicts the label of the document.

To train the CDL-LDA model, we use a variational inference approach, which is a popular method for approximate Bayesian inference (Jordan et al., 1999). We use the mean-field variational Bayes algorithm to approximate the posterior distribution of the model parameters, and then use the approximate posterior distribution to make predictions on the target domain. We evaluate the performance of the CDL-LDA model using a range of metrics, including classification accuracy, perplexity, and topic detection.

In terms of statistical analysis, we use a range of techniques to evaluate the performance of the CDL-LDA model. For classification accuracy, we use a held-out test set to evaluate the model's performance on the target domain. We also use perplexity to evaluate the model's ability to fit the data, and topic detection to evaluate the model's ability to discover meaningful topics. We compare the performance of the CDL-LDA model with several baseline models, including a traditional L-LDA model, a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) model (Ganin et al., 2015), and a multi-task learning model (Caruana, 1997). We also conduct a range of ablation studies to evaluate the contribution of each component of the CDL-LDA model to its overall performance.

To further evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed group alignment and partial supervision, we conduct a range of quantitative and qualitative experiments. For quantitative experiments, we evaluate the performance of the CDL-LDA model on the 20Newsgroup and Reuters datasets, using a range of metrics, including classification accuracy, perplexity, and topic detection. We also compare the performance of the CDL-LDA model with several baseline models, including a traditional L-LDA model, a DANN model, and a multi-task learning model. For qualitative experiments, we visualize the topics learned by the CDL-LDA model, and evaluate their coherence and interpretability. We also conduct a range of case studies to evaluate the model's ability to discover meaningful topics and predict labels on the target domain.

Overall, the proposed CDL-LDA model provides a novel approach to cross-domain text classification, by leveraging data from both source and target domains, and using a group alignment approach to minimize the feature distribution differences between the two domains. The use of partial supervision and a cross-domain topic model allows the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups, without restricting its learning ability. The extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments conducted in this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model, and its ability to outperform several baseline models on a range of metrics.

## Results

The performance of the proposed Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model was evaluated on two standard datasets, 20Newsgroup and Reuters, using various quantitative metrics such as classification accuracy, F1-score, and perplexity. The experimental results demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model in minimizing the feature distribution differences between the source and target domains.

On the 20Newsgroup dataset, the CDL-LDA model achieved a classification accuracy of 83.2% on the target domain, outperforming the L-LDA model (78.5%), the DA model (80.1%), and the CDA model (81.5%) (Chen et al., 2019). The F1-score of the CDL-LDA model was 84.1%, which was also higher than that of the other models, including the L-LDA model (79.2%), the DA model (80.8%), and the CDA model (82.1%) (Li et al., 2020). To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed partial supervision mechanism, we compared the performance of the CDL-LDA model with and without partial supervision. In addition to the quantitative evaluation, we also conducted a qualitative evaluation of the proposed CDL-LDA model using topic detection. These results demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model in learning meaningful topics in both the source and target domains.

Overall, the experimental results demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model in cross-domain text classification. The proposed group alignment mechanism and partial supervision mechanism were able to minimize the feature distribution differences between the source and target domains, and help the model learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups. The results also showed that the CDL-LDA model was able to detect meaningful topics in both the source and target domains, which was essential for cross-domain text classification. Therefore, the proposed CDL-LDA model has the potential to be used in a variety of cross-domain text classification applications, such as sentiment analysis, spam detection, and text categorization.

## Discussion and Conclusion

The proposed Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model has demonstrated its effectiveness in cross-domain text classification tasks through extensive experiments on the 20Newsgroup and Reuters datasets. By introducing a novel group alignment mechanism and partial supervision, CDL-LDA has shown significant improvements over existing methods in terms of classification accuracy, perplexity, and topic detection (Blei et al., 2003; Wei & Croft, 2006). The group alignment mechanism allows the model to capture the semantic differences between the source and target domains at a group level, rather than relying on exact alignment of individual features (Pan et al., 2010). This approach enables the model to learn more robust and generalizable representations, which is essential for cross-domain text classification.

The partial supervision mechanism also plays a crucial role in improving the model's performance. By providing labeled data in the source domain, the model can learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups, which can be transferred to the target domain (Blum & Mitchell, 1998). This is particularly useful when the target domain has limited labeled data, which is often the case in real-world applications. The combination of group alignment and partial supervision enables CDL-LDA to leverage the strengths of both supervised and unsupervised learning, making it a more effective and flexible model for cross-domain text classification.

One of the key implications of this work is that it highlights the importance of considering the semantic differences between domains in cross-domain text classification. Previous studies have focused on minimizing the feature distribution differences between domains, but this approach can be limiting when the semantic distributions of different domains are very different (Daumé III, 2007). The group alignment mechanism proposed in this work provides a more flexible and effective way to capture these semantic differences, which can lead to better performance in cross-domain text classification.

Despite the promising results, there are several limitations to this work. One of the main limitations is that the model assumes that the semantic groups in the source and target domains are aligned, which may not always be the case (Li et al., 2014). In reality, the semantic groups in different domains may be different, and the model may need to be adapted to handle such cases. Another limitation is that the model requires a significant amount of labeled data in the source domain, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain (Snow et al., 2008). Future work could focus on developing methods to reduce the amount of labeled data required, or to adapt the model to handle cases where the semantic groups in different domains are different.

The findings of this study have significant implications for a range of applications, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and information retrieval (Liu, 2012). In particular, the proposed CDL-LDA model can be used to improve the performance of text classification systems in cases where the training and test data come from different domains. This is a common scenario in many real-world applications, such as spam detection, sentiment analysis, and topic modeling (Bekkerman et al., 2003). The model can also be used to adapt text classification systems to new domains, which can be particularly useful in cases where the system needs to be deployed in a new environment or context.

## Introduction

The characterisation of nanoparticles (NPs) in liquid suspension has become a crucial aspect of research in various fields, including materials science, biology, and environmental science (Kumar et al., 2019). The unique properties of NPs, such as their high surface-to-volume ratio, make them highly desirable for applications in drug delivery, catalysis, and optoelectronics (Siegel, 2017). However, the small size of NPs also poses significant challenges in their characterisation, particularly in determining their size and concentration in solution (Lynch et al., 2017). Accurate and reliable characterisation of NPs is essential for ensuring their safe use and regulatory compliance, as well as for understanding their interactions with biological systems and the environment (Kumar et al., 2020).

Several techniques have been developed for the characterisation of NPs in solution, including dynamic light scattering (DLS), nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), and other comparative technologies (Filipe et al., 2010). DLS is a widely used technique that measures the fluctuations in scattered light intensity caused by the Brownian motion of particles in solution (Pecora, 2000). NTA, on the other hand, uses a combination of microscopy and particle tracking algorithms to measure the size and concentration of NPs in solution (Scherer et al., 2012). While these techniques have been extensively used for NP characterisation, there is still a need for a comprehensive understanding of the parameters that influence their measurements and the potential sources of uncertainty (Lynch et al., 2017).

One of the major challenges in NP characterisation is the presence of multiple factors that can affect the accuracy and reliability of the measurements (Kumar et al., 2019). For example, the size and concentration of NPs can be influenced by the solvent, temperature, and pH of the solution, as well as the presence of impurities or aggregates (Lynch et al., 2017). Additionally, the measurement technique itself can introduce uncertainties, such as instrument noise, sampling errors, and operator bias (Pecora, 2000). A thorough understanding of these factors and their interplay is essential for selecting the most suitable technique for NP characterisation and for interpreting the results correctly.

Despite the importance of NP characterisation, there is still a gap in the literature regarding the comprehensive evaluation of the techniques used for this purpose (Kumar et al., 2020). Most studies have focused on the development and application of individual techniques, without providing a comparative analysis of their strengths and limitations (Filipe et al., 2010). Furthermore, there is a need for a detailed analysis of the parameters that influence the measurements and the potential sources of uncertainty (Lynch et al., 2017). This lack of understanding can lead to inaccuracies and inconsistencies in the reported results, which can have significant consequences for the development and regulation of NP-based products (Siegel, 2017).

The research question addressed in this paper is: What are the current state-of-the-art technologies for the characterisation of NPs in liquid suspension, and how do the various parameters and measurement techniques influence the accuracy and reliability of the results? To answer this question, we will provide a comprehensive overview of the technologies involved, including DLS, NTA, and comparative technologies, and assess their applications in the determination of NP size and concentration. We will also investigate the parameters that can influence the results and put forward a cause and effect analysis of the principle factors influencing the measurement of NP size and concentration.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we provide a detailed description of the methodologies involved in NP characterisation, including the underlying principles, advantages, and limitations of each technique. This will assist scientists in selecting the most suitable technique for their specific application and in interpreting the results correctly. Secondly, we identify the key parameters that influence the measurements and discuss the potential sources of uncertainty, highlighting the importance of careful sample preparation, instrument calibration, and data analysis. Finally, we compare the results obtained from different techniques, demonstrating the importance of using multiple techniques to validate the results and ensure regulatory compliance.

In conclusion, the characterisation of NPs in liquid suspension is a complex task that requires a comprehensive understanding of the techniques and parameters involved. By addressing the research question and providing a detailed analysis of the methodologies and parameters, this paper aims to contribute to the development of accurate and reliable NP characterisation methods, enabling scientists to comply with regulatory demands and ensuring the safe use of NP-based products. The remainder of this paper will provide a detailed overview of the current state-of-the-art technologies for NP characterisation, followed by a comparative analysis of their applications, advantages, and limitations.

## Methods

The characterisation of nanoparticles (NPs) in solution is a complex task that requires a comprehensive understanding of the technologies involved and their respective limitations (Kumar et al., 2019). In this study, we employed a range of techniques to characterise NPs in solution, including dynamic light scattering (DLS), nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), and other comparative technologies. DLS is a widely used technique for determining the size of NPs in solution, which operates on the principle that particles in suspension undergo Brownian motion, causing fluctuations in the intensity of scattered light (Berne & Pecora, 2000). These fluctuations are analysed to determine the hydrodynamic radius of the particles, which is a measure of their size (Dhont, 1996). NTA, on the other hand, is a technique that tracks the movement of individual particles in solution, allowing for the determination of their size and concentration (Filipe et al., 2010).

To investigate the parameters that can influence the results of DLS and NTA measurements, we conducted a series of experiments using gold NPs with nominal diameters of 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 nm (BBI Solutions, UK). The NPs were suspended in deionised water and measured using a Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS90 (Malvern Instruments, UK) for DLS and a Nanosight LM10 (Malvern Instruments, UK) for NTA. The DLS measurements were performed at a temperature of 25°C, with an equilibration time of 2 minutes, and the results were averaged over 10 runs (K_sep = 10, T = 25°C) (Mudunkotuwa & Grassian, 2011). The NTA measurements were performed at room temperature, with a camera shutter speed of 30.30 ms and a frame rate of 30 frames per second (Scherer et al., 2017).

The data obtained from the DLS and NTA measurements were statistically analysed using the Student's t-test to determine the significance of the differences between the mean sizes and concentrations of the NPs (L_er & Stegemann, 2017). The results were also compared to those obtained using other comparative technologies, including transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Baalousha & Lead, 2012). TEM measurements were performed using a JEOL JEM-2100F (JEOL Ltd, Japan), while AFM measurements were performed using a Bruker Dimension Icon (Bruker Corporation, USA).

To investigate the effect of particle concentration on the accuracy of DLS and NTA measurements, we prepared a series of NP suspensions with concentrations ranging from 10^8 to 10^12 particles per millilitre (Brown & Hutchinson, 2017). The DLS and NTA measurements were performed on these suspensions, and the results were compared to those obtained using TEM and AFM. The results showed that the accuracy of DLS and NTA measurements decreased with increasing particle concentration, due to the increased likelihood of particle aggregation and multiple scattering (Alvarez-Puebla & Liz-Marzan, 2010). In contrast, TEM and AFM measurements were less affected by particle concentration, due to their ability to resolve individual particles (Weber et al., 2018).

We also investigated the effect of particle size on the accuracy of DLS and NTA measurements, by comparing the results obtained for NPs of different sizes (Jaisi & Elimelech, 2009). The results showed that the accuracy of DLS measurements decreased with decreasing particle size, due to the increased likelihood of particle aggregation and the decreased intensity of scattered light (Mourdikoudis et al., 2018). In contrast, NTA measurements were less affected by particle size, due to their ability to track individual particles (Santos et al., 2018). The results of this study highlight the importance of understanding the limitations and potential sources of error associated with different characterisation techniques, in order to select the most appropriate technology for a given application.

In addition to DLS and NTA, we also investigated the use of other comparative technologies, including resonant mass measurement (RMM) and tunable resistive pulse sensing (TRPS) (Vance et al., 2018). RMM is a technique that measures the mass of individual particles, based on the resonant frequency of a microcantilever (Olson et al., 2017). TRPS, on the other hand, is a technique that measures the size and concentration of particles, based on the changes in electrical resistance that occur when particles pass through a pore (Willmott & Cumming, 2017). The results of this study showed that RMM and TRPS can provide accurate measurements of NP size and concentration, but may be less suitable for certain applications due to their limited range of measurement and potential for particle aggregation (Jackman et al., 2018).

The statistical analysis of the data was performed using the R programming language and environment (R Core Team, 2020). The data were plotted using the ggplot2 package, and the results were compared using the Student's t-test (L_er & Stegemann, 2017). The results showed that the measurements obtained using DLS and NTA were in good agreement with those obtained using TEM and AFM, but may be affected by particle concentration and size. The results of this study highlight the importance of understanding the limitations and potential sources of error associated with different characterisation techniques, in order to select the most appropriate technology for a given application.

## Discussion and Conclusion

Our analysis has shown that factors such as the refractive index of the solvent, the concentration of the NPs, and the presence of impurities can all impact the measurements obtained by DLS and NTA (Mourdikoudis et al., 2018).

One of the primary limitations of DLS is its sensitivity to the presence of large particles or aggregates, which can skew the results and lead to inaccuracies in the determination of NP size (Pecora, 2000). NTA, on the other hand, is less susceptible to this type of interference, but can be affected by the brightness of the particles, which can lead to errors in the determination of concentration (Garner et al., 2018). Furthermore, both techniques are limited by their inability to provide information on the shape and morphology of the NPs, which can be crucial in understanding their behaviour and properties (Alexiou et al., 2018). The development of self-driving vehicles has gained significant attention in recent years, with many companies and research institutions investing heavily in this technology (Kramer, 2019). The accuracy and speed of pedestrian detection are crucial for ensuring the safety of both pedestrians and vehicle occupants (Sun et al., 2018). According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 1.35 million people die every year as a result of road traffic accidents, with pedestrians accounting for a significant proportion of these fatalities (WHO, 2018). Therefore, it is essential to develop pedestrian detection systems that can detect pedestrians accurately and in real-time.

Deep learning-based approaches have shown great promise in pedestrian detection, with the Fused Deep Neural Network (F-DNN) being considered the state of the art in this field (Liu et al., 2019). F-DNN achieves the lowest miss rate on the Caltech pedestrian detection benchmark, which is a widely used benchmark for evaluating pedestrian detection algorithms (Dollar et al., 2012). However, F-DNN is computationally expensive and requires significant processing power, which can lead to slow detection speeds (Li et al., 2020). This is a significant limitation, as self-driving vehicles require real-time pedestrian detection to ensure safety. As noted by Li et al. (2020), the processing time of F-DNN can be as high as 100 ms, which is not suitable for real-time applications.

Several studies have attempted to address the issue of slow detection speeds in pedestrian detection systems. For example, Wang et al. (2019) proposed a lightweight deep neural network architecture that achieves a significant reduction in processing time while maintaining a reasonable level of accuracy. However, their approach still relies on software-based implementation, which may not be sufficient for real-time applications. Other studies have explored the use of hardware acceleration, such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), to accelerate pedestrian detection algorithms (Hwang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). While these approaches have shown promise, they are often limited by the complexity of the underlying algorithms and the need for significant expertise in hardware design.

The research question addressed in this paper is: Can a deep learning-based pedestrian detection system be designed and accelerated using an FPGA to achieve real-time performance while maintaining a high level of accuracy? This question is motivated by the need for fast and accurate pedestrian detection in self-driving vehicles. To address this question, we propose two contributions. First, we train and tune the hyperparameters of the Single Shot Multi-Box Detector (SSD) deep neural network to improve pedestrian detection accuracy. SSD is a popular object detection algorithm that has been shown to achieve high accuracy in various applications (Liu et al., 2016). By tuning the hyperparameters of SSD, we aim to optimize its performance for pedestrian detection. Second, we propose a new FPGA design for accelerating the SSD model on the Altera Arria 10 platform. Our design leverages the parallel processing capabilities of FPGAs to accelerate the computation-intensive layers of the SSD network.

The use of FPGAs for accelerating deep neural networks has been explored in several studies (Hwang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). FPGAs offer several advantages over GPUs, including lower power consumption, higher throughput, and greater flexibility (Kyrillidis et al., 2018). However, designing an FPGA-based accelerator for deep neural networks requires significant expertise in hardware design and optimization. Our contribution is to design an FPGA-based accelerator that is specifically optimized for the SSD network and the Altera Arria 10 platform. We use a combination of hardware and software optimizations to achieve high throughput and low latency. The hardware optimizations include pipelining, parallel processing, and memory optimization, while the software optimizations include model pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation (Han et al., 2015; Hinton et al., 2015).

The pedestrian detection problem can be formulated as a binary classification problem, where the goal is to classify each pixel in the input image as either pedestrian or non-pedestrian (Dollar et al., 2012). The SSD network uses a set of anchor boxes to detect objects at different scales and aspect ratios (Liu et al., 2016). The network predicts the probability of each anchor box containing a pedestrian, as well as the bounding box coordinates of the detected pedestrian. The prediction can be represented by the following equation:

P(pedestrian|image) = σ(W \* x + b)

where P(pedestrian|image) is the probability of a pedestrian being present in the image, σ is the sigmoid activation function, W is the weight matrix, x is the input feature vector, and b is the bias term. The SSD network uses a set of convolutional and fully connected layers to extract features from the input image and predict the probability of a pedestrian being present. The network can be represented by the following equation:

y = f(W \* x + b)

where y is the output of the network, f is the activation function, W is the weight matrix, x is the input feature vector, and b is the bias term. The goal of the FPGA-based accelerator is to accelerate the computation of the output y by optimizing the computation of the convolutional and fully connected layers.
