The use of brief consultations and standard educational materials, as employed in the TUPD program, is a low-cost and efficient approach that can be easily replicated in other settings (Kumar et al., 2020). Furthermore, the involvement of pharmacists in medication management and adherence support can help to reduce the burden on primary care physicians and improve overall healthcare outcomes (Pellegrino et al., 2019).

This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. The sample size was relatively small, and the study was conducted in a single state, which may limit the generalizability of the findings (Gale et al., 2019). Additionally, the study relied on self-reported data from pharmacies, which may be subject to bias (Larkin et al., 2019). Future studies should aim to recruit larger samples and use more objective measures of adherence, such as electronic health records or claims data (Shrank et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of community pharmacies in improving adherence to blood pressure medication among patients in rural Montana. The TUPD program, which employed brief consultations and standard educational materials, was associated with significant improvements in adherence rates. The findings of this study have important implications for healthcare policy and practice, highlighting the potential of community pharmacies to play a key role in improving medication adherence and reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease. Further research is needed to replicate these findings in other settings and to explore the long-term sustainability of such interventions (Briesacher et al., 2019). Nevertheless, the results of this study provide strong evidence for the value of community pharmacies in promoting adherence to blood pressure medication and improving overall healthcare outcomes.

Introduction

The emergence of Big Data has revolutionized the way we process and analyze large volumes of data, with the map-reduce paradigm being a cornerstone of this revolution (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008). The ability to handle massive amounts of data in a distributed and scalable manner has made Big Data a popular choice for many applications, from social media analytics to scientific research (Lazer et al., 2014). However, the popularity of Big Data may not necessarily translate to suitability for all problems, particularly those that are time-dependent and require efficient processing of data in real-time (Laplante, 2017). The traditional map-reduce model, which relies on a batch processing approach, may not be the best fit for such problems, as it can lead to high latency and inefficient use of resources (Akidau et al., 2015).

The map-reduce paradigm, first introduced by Google (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008), is based on a simple and elegant idea of breaking down complex data processing tasks into smaller, independent chunks that can be processed in parallel. The map phase processes the input data in parallel, producing a set of key-value pairs, which are then shuffled and reduced to produce the final output (Lee et al., 2012). While this approach has been highly successful in processing large volumes of data, it has some inherent limitations, particularly when dealing with time-dependent data. The batch processing nature of map-reduce can lead to high latency, as the entire dataset needs to be processed before the results are available (Akidau et al., 2015). Furthermore, the use of caching and indexing can lead to significant overhead, particularly when dealing with high-volume and high-velocity data streams (Shah et al., 2017).

Despite these limitations, the Big Data approach has been widely adopted, partly due to its simplicity and scalability, and partly due to the buzzword value it holds for investors and clients (Lohr, 2012). However, as noted by (Laplante, 2017), popularity is not a measure of suitability, and the Big Data approach may not be the best solution for many common problems. In particular, time-dependent problems, such as real-time analytics, IoT data processing, and financial transaction processing, require efficient and timely processing of data, which may not be achievable using traditional map-reduce models (Akidau et al., 2015). These problems often involve processing large volumes of data in real-time, with low latency and high throughput requirements, making the traditional batch processing approach of map-reduce less suitable (Shah et al., 2017).

The gap in current research is the lack of a suitable framework for processing time-dependent data in a efficient and scalable manner. While several alternatives to map-reduce have been proposed, such as streaming processing and event-driven architectures (Akidau et al., 2015), these approaches often require significant changes to the underlying infrastructure and may not be compatible with existing Big Data systems (Laplante, 2017). Furthermore, the use of caching and indexing can lead to significant overhead, particularly when dealing with high-volume and high-velocity data streams (Shah et al., 2017). Therefore, there is a need for a new framework that can efficiently process time-dependent data in a scalable and timely manner, without requiring significant changes to the underlying infrastructure.

The research question that this paper aims to address is: Can a partly stateless, flow-oriented function and data model be used to substitute the traditional map-shuffle-reduce models for processing time-dependent data? In other words, can we design a framework that can efficiently process large volumes of time-dependent data in real-time, with low latency and high throughput requirements, using a partly stateless and flow-oriented approach? This question is motivated by the need for a more efficient and scalable approach to processing time-dependent data, which can take advantage of the latest advances in data processing and storage technologies (Laplante, 2017).

The contributions of this paper are twofold. Firstly, it presents a new framework for processing time-dependent data, based on a partly stateless, flow-oriented function and data model. This framework is designed to efficiently process large volumes of data in real-time, with low latency and high throughput requirements, making it suitable for a wide range of applications, from real-time analytics to IoT data processing. Secondly, it provides a detailed evaluation of the proposed framework, using a variety of benchmarks and case studies, to demonstrate its effectiveness and scalability. The proposed framework has the potential to revolutionize the way we process time-dependent data, enabling efficient and timely processing of large volumes of data, without requiring significant changes to the underlying infrastructure (Shah et al., 2017). By addressing the limitations of traditional map-reduce models and providing a more efficient and scalable approach to processing time-dependent data, this paper aims to contribute to the ongoing debate on the future of Big Data processing and analytics.

## Methods

The quest for a more efficient and effective data processing paradigm beyond the traditional map-reduce framework of Big Data led to the exploration of fast data concepts. This investigation involved a comprehensive analysis of existing literature on Big Data and its limitations, particularly in handling time-dependent problems (Lopez et al., 2018). It became apparent that the map-reduce approach, while powerful for batch processing and analysis of large datasets, may not be optimal for applications requiring real-time or near-real-time processing and decision-making (Wang et al., 2019). 

To address these limitations, we adopted a mixed-methods approach, combining theoretical modeling with practical implementation and testing. First, a thorough review of current data processing models and technologies was conducted to identify potential gaps and areas for improvement (Chen et al., 2020). This review highlighted the potential benefits of moving towards partly stateless, flow-oriented functions and data models, particularly for time-dependent problems (Kumar et al., 2019).

Next, we designed a novel data model that incorporates principles of flow-oriented programming and stateless processing to enhance the handling of dynamic and time-sensitive data (Lee et al., 2020). This model, termed "Fast Data Processing" (FDP), is based on a microservices architecture that facilitates the modular and scalable processing of data streams (Zhang et al., 2018). FDP leverages in-memory computing and caching mechanisms to minimize latency and optimize performance, enabling real-time analytics and decision-making capabilities (Kim et al., 2017).

A key component of the FDP model is its ability to integrate with various data sources and sinks, allowing for seamless data ingestion, processing, and output (Patel et al., 2019). This is achieved through the use of standardized APIs and data protocols, ensuring interoperability and flexibility (Singh et al., 2020). Furthermore, FDP incorporates advanced analytics and machine learning capabilities, enabling the extraction of insights and patterns from fast-moving data streams (Gupta et al., 2018).

To validate the effectiveness of the FDP model, we conducted a series of experiments and benchmarks against traditional map-reduce-based systems (Sharma et al., 2019). These experiments involved processing large-scale datasets with varying levels of complexity and time-sensitivity, simulating real-world scenarios such as financial transactions, sensor data, and social media feeds (Jain et al., 2020). The results of these experiments were analyzed using statistical methods, including regression analysis and hypothesis testing, to compare the performance and efficiency of the FDP model against its Big Data counterparts (Bhatia et al., 2018).

Statistical analysis revealed significant improvements in processing speed and latency reduction when using the FDP model, particularly for time-dependent problems (p < 0.01) (Kaur et al., 2019). Additionally, the FDP model demonstrated better scalability and fault tolerance compared to traditional map-reduce systems, handling increased data volumes and velocities without significant performance degradation (Soni et al., 2020). These findings suggest that the FDP model offers a viable alternative to Big Data approaches for applications requiring fast data processing and real-time analytics.

The design and implementation of the FDP model also considered issues of data quality, security, and governance (Rao et al., 2018). Mechanisms for data validation, encryption, and access control were integrated into the model to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of processed data (Verma et al., 2019). Furthermore, the FDP model was designed to comply with relevant data regulations and standards, such as GDPR and HIPAA, providing a secure and trustworthy environment for fast data processing (Agrawal et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the methods employed in this research involved a comprehensive analysis of existing data processing paradigms, the design and implementation of a novel fast data processing model, and the conduct of rigorous experiments and statistical analysis to validate its effectiveness. The results of this study provide strong evidence for the potential of fast data processing models to overcome the limitations of traditional Big Data approaches, particularly in handling time-dependent problems and applications requiring real-time analytics and decision-making.

## Results

The experimental results of our proposed model, which we term "Fast Data," demonstrate a significant improvement in performance compared to traditional Big Data approaches, particularly in time-dependent problems (Kumar et al., 2019). Our model's ability to handle partly stateless, flow-oriented functions and data models allows for more efficient processing of real-time data streams (Lopez et al., 2020). In our experiments, we observed a reduction in processing time of up to 75% compared to traditional map-reduce models (Gupta et al., 2018). Specifically, our model was able to process 10,000 data points in 1.2 seconds, whereas the traditional map-reduce model took 4.8 seconds to process the same amount of data (p < 0.01) (Kumar et al., 2019).

In terms of throughput, our model was able to handle 50,000 data points per second, whereas the traditional model was only able to handle 20,000 data points per second (Lopez et al., 2020). This represents a 150% increase in throughput, which is significant for applications that require real-time processing of large amounts of data (Gupta et al., 2018). Furthermore, our model was able to maintain a consistent processing time of 1.2 seconds even when the data stream was increased to 100,000 data points, whereas the traditional model's processing time increased to 12.1 seconds (p < 0.001) (Kumar et al., 2019).

We also evaluated the performance of our model in terms of memory usage, which is an important consideration for large-scale data processing applications (Lopez et al., 2020). Our results show that our model uses significantly less memory than traditional map-reduce models, with an average memory usage of 1.5 GB compared to 5.2 GB for the traditional model (Gupta et al., 2018). This represents a 71% reduction in memory usage, which can be significant for applications that require processing of large amounts of data (Kumar et al., 2019).

In addition to the performance benefits, our model also provides a more scalable architecture for large-scale data processing applications (Lopez et al., 2020). Our results show that our model can scale to handle large amounts of data with minimal increase in processing time, whereas traditional map-reduce models require significant increases in computational resources to handle large amounts of data (Gupta et al., 2018). Specifically, our model was able to scale to handle 1 million data points with only a 10% increase in processing time, whereas the traditional model required a 500% increase in computational resources to handle the same amount of data (p < 0.001) (Kumar et al., 2019).

We also evaluated the performance of our model in terms of fault tolerance, which is an important consideration for large-scale data processing applications (Lopez et al., 2020). Our results show that our model is more fault-tolerant than traditional map-reduce models, with an average recovery time of 2.1 seconds compared to 10.5 seconds for the traditional model (Gupta et al., 2018). This represents a 80% reduction in recovery time, which can be significant for applications that require high availability and reliability (Kumar et al., 2019).

In terms of the types of applications that can benefit from our model, we found that any application that requires real-time processing of large amounts of data can benefit from our approach (Lopez et al., 2020). Specifically, applications such as financial analytics, sensor data processing, and social media analytics can benefit from our model's ability to handle partly stateless, flow-oriented functions and data models (Gupta et al., 2018). Our results show that our model can provide significant improvements in performance, scalability, and fault tolerance for these types of applications, making it a viable alternative to traditional Big Data approaches (Kumar et al., 2019).

Introduction

The loss of an upper limb can have a profound impact on an individual's quality of life, affecting their ability to perform daily activities, maintain independence, and engage in social and recreational pursuits (Biddiss & Chau, 2007). Upper extremity amputations can result from various causes, including trauma, cancer, congenital conditions, and vascular disease (Esquenazi, 2014). The prevalence of upper limb amputations is significant, with estimates suggesting that approximately 185,000 individuals in the United States alone are living with an upper limb amputation (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2008). The rehabilitation of upper extremity amputees is a complex and multifaceted process, requiring a comprehensive approach that addresses the physical, emotional, and social needs of the individual (Hill, 2017).

Prosthetic rehabilitation is a critical component of the rehabilitation process for upper extremity amputees, enabling individuals to regain functional ability and independence (Sullivan et al., 2018). The goal of prosthetic rehabilitation is to provide the individual with a prosthetic device that is functional, comfortable, and aesthetically pleasing, and to teach the individual how to use the device to perform daily activities (Lake, 2008). However, the rehabilitation process can be challenging, and individuals may experience difficulties with prosthetic fitting, training, and adaptation (Biddiss & Chau, 2007). Furthermore, the rehabilitation process can be influenced by a range of factors, including the level and cause of amputation, the individual's overall health and well-being, and their access to rehabilitation services (Esquenazi, 2014).

Despite the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees, there is a lack of comprehensive and systematic reviews of the literature on this topic (Sullivan et al., 2018). Many studies have investigated specific aspects of prosthetic rehabilitation, such as prosthetic design and fitting (Lake, 2008), prosthetic training and education (Biddiss & Chau, 2007), and the psychological and social impact of upper limb amputation (Hill, 2017). However, there is a need for a systematic and comprehensive review of the literature to identify the key components of effective prosthetic rehabilitation protocols for upper extremity amputees. This gap in the literature is significant, as it can limit the ability of rehabilitation professionals to provide evidence-based care and can hinder the development of effective rehabilitation protocols (Esquenazi, 2014).

The research question guiding this systematic review is: What are the key components of effective prosthetic rehabilitation protocols for upper extremity amputees? This question is important, as it can help to identify the essential elements of rehabilitation that are necessary to promote optimal outcomes for individuals with upper limb amputations (Sullivan et al., 2018). By addressing this research question, this systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the literature on prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees, and to identify the key components of effective rehabilitation protocols.

The contributions of this systematic review are several. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive and systematic review of the literature on prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees, which can help to identify the key components of effective rehabilitation protocols (Esquenazi, 2014). Secondly, it highlights the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to rehabilitation, involving a range of healthcare professionals, including prosthetists, occupational therapists, physical therapists, and psychologists (Hill, 2017). Thirdly, it emphasizes the need for individualized rehabilitation protocols that take into account the unique needs and circumstances of each individual (Biddiss & Chau, 2007). Finally, it provides a foundation for the development of evidence-based guidelines for prosthetic rehabilitation, which can help to promote optimal outcomes for individuals with upper limb amputations (Sullivan et al., 2018).

The importance of prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees cannot be overstated. Prosthetic rehabilitation can enable individuals to regain functional ability and independence, and to participate fully in daily activities and social pursuits (Lake, 2008). However, the rehabilitation process can be complex and challenging, and individuals may experience difficulties with prosthetic fitting, training, and adaptation (Biddiss & Chau, 2007). By providing a comprehensive overview of the literature on prosthetic rehabilitation, this systematic review aims to promote a better understanding of the key components of effective rehabilitation protocols, and to inform the development of evidence-based guidelines for rehabilitation practice (Esquenazi, 2014). Ultimately, the goal of this systematic review is to improve outcomes for individuals with upper limb amputations, and to enhance their quality of life and overall well-being (Hill, 2017).

In conclusion, the rehabilitation of upper extremity amputees is a complex and multifaceted process, requiring a comprehensive approach that addresses the physical, emotional, and social needs of the individual (Hill, 2017). Prosthetic rehabilitation is a critical component of the rehabilitation process, enabling individuals to regain functional ability and independence (Sullivan et al., 2018). This systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the literature on prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees, and to identify the key components of effective rehabilitation protocols. By addressing the research question and highlighting the contributions of this review, it is hoped that this systematic review will promote a better understanding of the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees, and will inform the development of evidence-based guidelines for rehabilitation practice (Esquenazi, 2014).

## Methods

This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA Statement 2009, which provides a framework for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Moher et al., 2009). The review aimed to evaluate the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation concerning upper extremity amputees. A comprehensive literature search was performed using multiple databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, to identify relevant studies concerning prosthetic rehabilitation in upper extremity amputees.

The search strategy involved using a combination of keywords and MeSH terms related to upper extremity amputees, prosthetic rehabilitation, and rehabilitation protocols. The keywords used included "upper extremity amputee," "prosthetic rehabilitation," "rehabilitation protocols," "amputation," "prosthetic training," and "rehabilitation outcomes." The search was limited to English language studies published between 2000 and 2022. The search strategy was designed to capture a broad range of studies, including randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and review articles.

The literature search identified 620 studies, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility. The inclusion criteria for this review were studies that (1) focused on upper extremity amputees, (2) evaluated prosthetic rehabilitation protocols, and (3) reported outcomes related to rehabilitation. Studies that did not meet these criteria, such as those focusing on lower extremity amputees or non-prosthetic rehabilitation, were excluded. The exclusion criteria also included studies with incomplete data, non-English language studies, and studies published before 2000.

The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the PEDro scale, which is a widely used tool for evaluating the quality of randomized controlled trials and observational studies (Maher et al., 2003). The PEDro scale assesses studies based on criteria such as randomization, blinding, and follow-up, and provides a score out of 10. Studies with a PEDro score of 6 or higher were considered to be of high methodological quality.

Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which included information on study design, sample size, population characteristics, rehabilitation protocols, and outcomes. The forms were completed by two independent reviewers, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus. The data extracted from the included studies were then synthesized and analyzed to identify common themes and patterns related to prosthetic rehabilitation protocols and outcomes.

The statistical analysis of the data was limited due to the heterogeneity of the included studies. However, descriptive statistics were used to summarize the characteristics of the included studies and the outcomes reported. The results of the review were then narratively synthesized to provide an overview of the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation concerning upper extremity amputees.

The search and screening process was performed by two independent reviewers, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus. The reviewers were not blinded to the authors or journals, as this information was considered to be relevant to the evaluation of the studies. The studies that met the inclusion criteria were then evaluated in more detail, and the data were extracted and analyzed as described above.

The use of the PRISMA Statement 2009 provided a framework for reporting the systematic review and ensured that the review was conducted in a transparent and rigorous manner (Moher et al., 2009). The PRISMA Statement 2009 includes a 27-item checklist, which covers aspects such as the background, methods, results, and discussion. The use of this checklist ensured that the review was conducted and reported in accordance with established guidelines.

Overall, the methods used in this systematic review were designed to provide a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation of the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation concerning upper extremity amputees. The use of a systematic search strategy, clear inclusion and exclusion criteria, and a standardized data extraction form ensured that the review was conducted in a transparent and reproducible manner. The evaluation of the methodological quality of the included studies using the PEDro scale provided an indication of the reliability and validity of the findings. The narrative synthesis of the results provided an overview of the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation concerning upper extremity amputees and highlighted areas for future research.

## Results

The systematic literature search yielded a total of 620 studies, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility based on the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria (Higgins & Green, 2011). After removing duplicates and studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria, 9 studies were selected for data extraction and analysis (Moher et al., 2009). These studies were published between 2010 and 2022, with the majority being published in the last five years, indicating a growing interest in the field of upper extremity prosthetic rehabilitation.

The 9 included studies involved a total of 427 participants, with a mean age of 34.6 years (SD = 10.2) and a male-to-female ratio of 2.5:1 (Sullivan et al., 2018). The most common cause of amputation was trauma (63.1%), followed by congenital conditions (21.5%) and vascular diseases (15.4%) (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2017). The level of amputation varied, with 42.2% being transradial, 31.4% being transhumeral, and 26.4% being shoulder disarticulation or forequarter amputations (Esquenazi, 2014).

The studies identified a range of prosthetic rehabilitation protocols, with the most common components being general exercise programs (77.8%), motor tasks (66.7%), phantom exercises (55.6%), and Muscle Training System (44.4%) (Hill et al., 2016). Edema control was also a common component, with 33.3% of the studies incorporating this into their rehabilitation protocols (Lake & Dodson, 2018). Functional activities, such as cooking and dressing, were included in 22.2% of the studies, while signal strengthening and prosthetic education exercises were each included in 11.1% of the studies (Skiakis & Koutsogiannis, 2019).

Neuromuscular reeducation was a component of 55.6% of the studies, with virtual image and virtual reality exercises being included in 22.2% and 11.1% of the studies, respectively (Conte et al., 2020). The duration of the rehabilitation programs varied, with a mean duration of 12.6 weeks (SD = 6.3) and a range of 4-24 weeks (Schofield et al., 2018). The frequency of rehabilitation sessions also varied, with a mean frequency of 2.5 sessions per week (SD = 1.1) and a range of 1-5 sessions per week (Wurdeman et al., 2019).

The outcomes measured in the studies included functional ability, prosthetic use, and quality of life, with 66.7% of the studies using standardized outcome measures such as the Southampton Hand Assessment Procedure (SHAP) and the Trinity Amputation and Prosthetic Experience Scales (TAPES) (Megari, 2013). The results of the studies showed significant improvements in functional ability and prosthetic use, with a mean increase in SHAP score of 14.5 points (SD = 6.2) and a mean increase in TAPES score of 10.2 points (SD = 4.5) (Kamenov et al., 2020).

The studies also reported high levels of patient satisfaction, with 85.7% of the studies reporting a mean satisfaction score of 85.1% (SD = 8.5) (Stanovic et al., 2019). The dropout rate was relatively low, with a mean dropout rate of 12.1% (SD = 6.3) and a range of 0-25% (Biddiss et al., 2017). The adverse event rate was also low, with a mean adverse event rate of 5.6% (SD = 3.1) and a range of 0-10% (Resnik & Klinger, 2018).

Overall, the results of this systematic review suggest that prosthetic rehabilitation is a promising approach for improving functional ability, prosthetic use, and quality of life in upper extremity amputees. The wide range of rehabilitation protocols and outcomes measured in the studies highlights the need for further research to determine the most effective components and dosage of rehabilitation programs for this population (Dawson et al., 2019).

## Discussion and Conclusion

The systematic review highlights the significance of prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees, underscoring the importance of a comprehensive rehabilitation protocol that encompasses a variety of exercises and training methods. The studies included in this review demonstrate that prosthetic rehabilitation can significantly improve the functional abilities and quality of life of individuals with upper limb amputations (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Seymour, 2008). The rehabilitation protocols identified in the literature, including general exercise programs, motor tasks, phantom exercises, and prosthetic education exercises, suggest a multifaceted approach to rehabilitation that addresses the physical, psychological, and functional needs of upper extremity amputees (Huang et al., 2015; Resnik et al., 2012).

The emphasis on early rehabilitation and the use of advanced technologies, such as virtual reality and muscle training systems, is noteworthy (CDecode et al., 2018; Pulliam et al., 2011). These technologies have been shown to enhance motor learning, improve prosthetic control, and reduce phantom limb pain, ultimately leading to better functional outcomes and increased patient satisfaction (Bertoni et al., 2017; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2016). Furthermore, the inclusion of neuromuscular reeducation and signal strengthening exercises in rehabilitation protocols highlights the importance of addressing the neurological and muscular adaptations that occur following amputation (Farina et al., 2018; Kuiken et al., 2009).

The findings of this review have significant implications for clinical practice and rehabilitation service delivery. Clinicians and rehabilitation professionals should prioritize the development of individualized rehabilitation plans that incorporate a range of exercises and training methods, taking into account the unique needs and goals of each patient (Esquenazi, 2014; Micera et al., 2010). Moreover, the integration of advanced technologies and innovative rehabilitation approaches should be encouraged, as these have the potential to enhance patient outcomes and improve the overall effectiveness of rehabilitation services (Blank et al., 2019; Pulliam et al., 2019).

Despite the promising findings of this review, there are several limitations that should be acknowledged. The relatively small number of studies included in the review, combined with the heterogeneity of the study designs and methodologies, may limit the generalizability of the results (Higgins & Green, 2011). Additionally, the review highlights the need for further research into the effectiveness and efficacy of specific rehabilitation interventions and protocols, particularly in the context of upper extremity amputations (Seymour, 2008). The lack of standardization in rehabilitation protocols and outcome measures also presents a challenge for clinicians and researchers, highlighting the need for further development and validation of standardized assessment tools and treatment guidelines (Resnik et al., 2012).

In conclusion, the current systematic review underscores the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation for upper extremity amputees, highlighting the need for comprehensive and individualized rehabilitation protocols that incorporate a range of exercises and training methods. The findings of this review have significant implications for clinical practice and rehabilitation service delivery, emphasizing the importance of prioritizing patient-centered care and incorporating innovative rehabilitation approaches and technologies. While limitations exist, the review provides a foundation for further research and highlights the need for continued development and refinement of rehabilitation protocols and services for individuals with upper limb amputations. Ultimately, the goal of prosthetic rehabilitation should be to optimize functional abilities, improve quality of life, and enhance overall well-being for individuals with upper extremity amputations, and this review provides a critical step towards achieving this goal.

Introduction

The introduction of biosimilar versions of widely prescribed biologic drugs has transformed the pharmaceutical landscape, offering patients and healthcare systems more affordable treatment options (Dorner et al., 2016). One such biologic drug is infliximab, a tumour-necrosis factor antagonist used to treat various inflammatory disorders, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis (Maini et al., 1999; Hanauer et al., 2002; Antoni et al., 2002). The reference product, Remicade, has been available since 1998, and several biosimilar versions have been approved in recent years, including Inflectra and Renflexis (Weise et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2018). Biosimilars are not identical copies of reference products, but rather highly similar versions that have undergone rigorous testing to demonstrate their similarity in terms of quality, safety, and efficacy (Schneider, 2013). As a result, there is a need to establish the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab, particularly in patients with chronic inflammatory disorders who may require long-term treatment (Faccin et al., 2017).

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued guidance on the development of biosimilars, including the requirement for studies to demonstrate interchangeability between a reference biologic and its biosimilar (FDA, 2015). Interchangeability refers to the ability to switch between a reference product and a biosimilar without affecting the safety or efficacy of treatment (Christl, 2017). To establish interchangeability, studies must demonstrate that biosimilars remain equivalent or non-inferior to a reference product after multiple switches between products (FDA, 2017). This requirement is crucial, as switching between biologic products may pose risks, such as changes in immunogenicity, efficacy, or safety profiles (Ebbers et al., 2012). However, the current evidence base for switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab is limited, and there is a need for a comprehensive review of the available data (Faccin et al., 2017).

The gap in the current literature is the lack of systematic reviews that evaluate the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab in patients with inflammatory disorders. While several studies have reported on the safety and efficacy of biosimilar infliximab in patients who have never received the reference product, few studies have investigated the effects of switching between the two products (Yoo et al., 2013; Park et al., 2013). Moreover, the available studies are mostly observational and uncontrolled, which limits their ability to establish causality and detect potential risks associated with switching (Gartlehner et al., 2017). Therefore, there is a need for a systematic review that synthesizes the available evidence on the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab, including data from randomized controlled trials and observational studies.

The research question guiding this systematic review is: What is the efficacy and safety of switching patients between reference and biosimilar infliximab in patients with inflammatory disorders, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis? This review aims to investigate the available evidence on the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab, including data on immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety outcomes. The review will also examine the quality of the available evidence and identify gaps in the current literature, including the need for randomized controlled trials and long-term follow-up data.

This systematic review will contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive overview of the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab. The review will help to inform clinicians, patients, and healthcare policymakers about the potential risks and benefits of switching between these products, which is essential for making informed decisions about treatment (Dorner et al., 2016). Additionally, the review will identify areas for future research, including the need for randomized controlled trials and long-term follow-up data, which will help to establish the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab (Gartlehner et al., 2017). Overall, this systematic review will provide a critical evaluation of the available evidence on the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab, which will help to promote the safe and effective use of biosimilars in clinical practice.

## Methods

The methodology employed in this systematic review was designed to comprehensively identify and evaluate the existing evidence on the efficacy and safety of switching patients between reference and biosimilar infliximab. To achieve this, a thorough search of the literature was conducted, utilizing multiple databases and congress abstracts to ensure a wide coverage of published and unpublished data. The search strategy was developed in consultation with a librarian and included terms related to infliximab, biosimilars, switching, and the conditions of interest, such as Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis (Lefebvre et al., 2019).

The MEDLINE database was searched for published studies using a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms. The search terms included "infliximab," "biosimilar," "switching," "Crohn's disease," "ulcerative colitis," "rheumatoid arthritis," "ankylosing spondylitis," "psoriatic arthritis," and "plaque psoriasis" (Higgins & Green, 2011). The EMBASE database was also searched for congress abstracts, and manual searches were conducted of abstracts from relevant congresses, including those of the European Crohn's and Colitis Organisation, the American Gastroenterological Association, the American College of Rheumatology, and the European League Against Rheumatism (Boutron et al., 2014).

Studies were eligible for inclusion if they presented data on switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab in patients with inflammatory disorders. No language restrictions were applied, and both published and unpublished studies were considered. However, studies with fewer than 10 patients were excluded, as were those that did not report on the safety and efficacy of switching (Moher et al., 2009). The search results were screened by two independent reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer (Higgins & Green, 2011).

A total of 113 journal articles and 149 abstracts were identified through the search strategy. After screening, 70 studies were considered relevant and included in the analysis. The majority of the included studies were uncontrolled, observational studies, which reported on the outcomes of patients who had switched from reference to biosimilar infliximab or vice versa (Golder et al., 2016). Data from six randomized, controlled trials were also identified, which compared the efficacy and safety of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab with continuing reference infliximab (Schulz et al., 2010).

The data extracted from the included studies included patient demographics, disease characteristics, switching regimen, and outcomes, such as clinical response, remission rates, and adverse events (Stewart et al., 2015). The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies and the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for randomized, controlled trials (Wells et al., 2014; Higgins et al., 2011). The quality assessment was performed by two independent reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer.

Statistical analysis was not performed due to the heterogeneity of the included studies and the lack of standardized outcome measures (Higgins & Green, 2011). Instead, a narrative synthesis of the findings was conducted, which involved a descriptive summary of the results, including the study characteristics, patient demographics, and outcomes (Popay et al., 2006). The narrative synthesis was used to identify patterns and trends in the data and to explore the relationships between the study characteristics and outcomes.

The findings of this systematic review were interpreted in the context of the current evidence on biosimilars and switching, as well as the regulatory requirements for demonstrating interchangeability (US Food and Drug Administration, 2019). The implications of the findings for clinical practice and future research were also considered, including the need for additional studies to explore the potential risks and benefits of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab in various populations and scenarios (Ebbers et al., 2019). Overall, the methodology employed in this systematic review was designed to provide a comprehensive and transparent evaluation of the existing evidence on the efficacy and safety of switching patients between reference and biosimilar infliximab.

## Results

A comprehensive search of the MEDLINE database yielded a total of 113 journal articles, while the EMBASE database and manual searches of relevant congress abstracts resulted in 149 abstracts (Yoo et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020). After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 70 publications were deemed relevant and included in this analysis (Jørgensen et al., 2019; Gecse et al., 2020). The majority of these publications, approximately 80%, were uncontrolled, observational studies, highlighting the need for more rigorous, controlled trials to assess the efficacy and safety of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab (Cohen et al., 2020; Fiorino et al., 2020).

Data from six randomised, controlled trials (RCTs) were identified, providing higher levels of evidence compared to observational studies (Barkham et al., 2020; Kolar et al., 2020). These RCTs enrolled a total of 1,463 patients with various inflammatory disorders, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis (Papp et al., 2020; Schreiber et al., 2020). The sample sizes of the RCTs ranged from 100 to 500 patients, with the largest study being the NOR-SWITCH trial, which included 482 patients (Jørgensen et al., 2017).

In terms of efficacy, the RCTs generally demonstrated that switching from reference infliximab to biosimilar infliximab did not result in significant changes in disease activity or clinical response (Cohen et al., 2020; Fiorino et al., 2020). For example, the NOR-SWITCH trial reported that 99.4% of patients maintained clinical response after switching from reference infliximab to biosimilar infliximab (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Similarly, the CT-P13 trial demonstrated that 93.5% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis maintained their clinical response after switching to biosimilar infliximab (Yoo et al., 2017).

Safety data from the RCTs and observational studies revealed no clinically important safety signals associated with switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab (Barkham et al., 2020; Kolar et al., 2020). The incidence of adverse events, including serious adverse events, was similar between patients who switched to biosimilar infliximab and those who continued to receive reference infliximab (Papp et al., 2020; Schreiber et al., 2020). For instance, a study by Gecse et al. (2020) reported that the incidence of adverse events was 24.1% in the switch group versus 25.6% in the non-switch group.

Immunogenicity data, which are crucial for assessing the potential impact of switching on the immune system, were available from four of the RCTs (Cohen et al., 2020; Fiorino et al., 2020). These data indicated that switching from reference infliximab to biosimilar infliximab did not result in significant changes in anti-drug antibody levels or neutralizing antibody levels (Jørgensen et al., 2017; Yoo et al., 2017). However, it is essential to note that the follow-up periods in these studies were relatively short, ranging from 16 to 52 weeks, which may not be sufficient to capture potential long-term immunogenicity effects (Barkham et al., 2020; Kolar et al., 2020).

Observational studies, although limited by their study design, provided valuable real-world data on the efficacy and safety of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab (Gecse et al., 2020; Papp et al., 2020). A study by Schreiber et al. (2020) reported on a cohort of 1,012 patients with inflammatory bowel disease who switched from reference infliximab to biosimilar infliximab, with a median follow-up of 12 months. The study found that 85.1% of patients maintained clinical remission after switching, with no significant increase in adverse events or immunogenicity.

While the available data have not identified significant risks associated with a single switch between reference and biosimilar infliximab, it is crucial to acknowledge the limitations of the current evidence (Cohen et al., 2020; Fiorino et al., 2020). Most of the studies reported on only single switches, and the majority were observational studies lacking control arms (Jørgensen et al., 2019; Gecse et al., 2020). Furthermore, the follow-up periods in these studies were relatively short, which may not be sufficient to capture potential long-term effects of switching (Barkham et al., 2020; Kolar et al., 2020). Additional data are needed to explore potential switching risks in various populations and scenarios, including multiple switches, switching in patients with different disease states, and switching in patients with a history of immunogenicity or adverse events (Papp et al., 2020; Schreiber et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the available evidence suggests that switching from reference infliximab to biosimilar infliximab is not associated with significant changes in efficacy or safety (Cohen et al., 2020; Fiorino et al., 2020). However, the limitations of the current evidence highlight the need for further studies to establish the long-term safety and efficacy of switching between these products (Jørgensen et al., 2019; Gecse et al., 2020). Future studies should aim to address these knowledge gaps and provide more comprehensive data on the effects of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab in various patient populations and scenarios (Barkham et al., 2020; Kolar et al., 2020).

## Discussion and Conclusion

The systematic review of the efficacy and safety of switching patients between reference and biosimilar infliximab reveals that the available evidence does not indicate significant risks associated with a single switch between these products (Cohen et al., 2018; Glintborg et al., 2019). The majority of the studies included in this analysis were uncontrolled, observational studies, which may be subject to biases and limitations (Benucci et al., 2019). However, the data from six randomised, controlled trials provide more robust evidence, and these studies also suggest that switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab does not result in clinically important efficacy or safety signals (Jørgensen et al., 2017; Park et al., 2019).

One of the key limitations of the current evidence is that most studies only report on single switches between reference and biosimilar infliximab (Cohen et al., 2018). This is a significant limitation, as the US Food and Drug Administration guidance states that studies must demonstrate that biosimilars remain equivalent or non-inferior to a reference product after multiple switches between products (US FDA, 2019). Therefore, further studies are needed to explore the potential risks associated with multiple switches between reference and biosimilar infliximab. Additionally, the current evidence is mostly based on studies conducted in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and more data are needed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of switching in patients with other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis (Glintborg et al., 2019).

The lack of control arms in most of the observational studies included in this analysis is another significant limitation (Benucci et al., 2019). Control arms are essential to provide a comparator group, which allows for the evaluation of the efficacy and safety of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab. Without control arms, it is challenging to determine whether any observed effects are due to the switch or other factors, such as the natural course of the disease (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Therefore, future studies should include control arms to provide more robust evidence.

Despite these limitations, the available evidence suggests that switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab is not associated with significant risks (Cohen et al., 2018; Glintborg et al., 2019). This is an important finding, as it may help to increase confidence in the use of biosimilars and reduce costs associated with the treatment of inflammatory disorders (Park et al., 2019). However, it is essential to continue monitoring the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab, particularly in patients who undergo multiple switches (US FDA, 2019).

The implications of this systematic review are significant, as they may inform clinical practice and policy decisions (Benucci et al., 2019). The findings suggest that switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab may be a viable option for patients with inflammatory disorders, particularly in situations where cost is a significant factor (Glintborg et al., 2019). However, it is essential to consider the individual patient's circumstances and medical history before making a decision to switch (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Additionally, healthcare professionals should continue to monitor patients who switch between reference and biosimilar infliximab, as the long-term effects of switching are not yet fully understood (Cohen et al., 2018).

In conclusion, while the available evidence does not indicate significant risks associated with a single switch between reference and biosimilar infliximab, further studies are needed to explore potential switching risks in various populations and scenarios (US FDA, 2019). The limitations of the current evidence, including the lack of control arms and the focus on single switches, highlight the need for more robust studies to evaluate the safety and efficacy of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab (Benucci et al., 2019). Nevertheless, the findings of this systematic review may help to increase confidence in the use of biosimilars and inform clinical practice and policy decisions (Glintborg et al., 2019). Ultimately, the goal of this research is to provide high-quality evidence to support the safe and effective use of biosimilars, which may help to improve patient outcomes and reduce healthcare costs (Park et al., 2019).

## Introduction

The role of entrepreneurship in academic research has garnered significant attention in recent years, with a growing body of literature exploring the intersection of entrepreneurial orientation and research productivity (e.g., Kirzner, 1982; Shane & Venkataraman, 2000). Entrepreneurial orientation (EO) refers to the propensity of individuals or organizations to engage in innovative, proactive, and risk-taking behaviors (Miller, 1983; Covin & Wales, 2012). In the context of academic research, EO may manifest in the adoption of novel methodologies, the exploration of new research areas, or the application of innovative technologies to address complex problems (Burgelman, 1983; Venkataraman, 1997). However, the extent to which academics exhibit entrepreneurial tendencies, and the impact of such tendencies on research productivity, remains poorly understood (Kuratko, 2005; Bae et al., 2014).

Research productivity is a critical aspect of academic performance, as it contributes to the advancement of knowledge, the development of innovative solutions, and the improvement of societal well-being (Merton, 1973; Latour, 1987). In the higher education sector, research productivity is often measured by the number of publications, citations, and research grants secured by academics (Fox, 1983; Long & McGinnis, 1985). While numerous factors have been identified as influencing research productivity, including individual characteristics, institutional factors, and disciplinary differences (e.g., Reskin, 1977; Allison & Long, 1990), the role of entrepreneurial orientation remains a relatively unexplored area of inquiry.

One of the key challenges in examining the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation and research productivity is the notion that academic research is often conducted within established paradigms or frameworks (Kuhn, 1962; Lakatos, 1970). This implies that certain research areas may be less amenable to innovative or entrepreneurial approaches, as they are bound by established methodologies and theoretical perspectives (Fuchs & Turner, 1986; Becher, 1989). However, this perspective overlooks the potential for academics to apply novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, to enhance their research productivity (Howell, 2015; Cordes-Berszinn, 2017). The increasing availability of digital platforms and tools has created new opportunities for academics to engage in collaborative, open, and innovative research practices (Nielsen, 2012; Waldman, 2017).

Despite the growing recognition of the importance of entrepreneurial orientation in academic research, there is a significant gap in our understanding of the relationship between EO and research productivity. Existing studies have primarily focused on the individual characteristics of entrepreneurs, such as personality traits and cognitive styles, rather than their academic counterparts (e.g., Shaver & Scott, 1991; Stewart & Roth, 2001). Furthermore, the majority of research on academic entrepreneurship has been conducted in developed-country contexts, with limited attention paid to the specific challenges and opportunities faced by academics in developing countries (e.g., Altbach, 2004; Cloete et al., 2015).

This study seeks to address this gap by exploring the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity in a developing-country context. The research question guiding this investigation is: To what extent do academics with higher levels of entrepreneurial orientation and technological propensity exhibit higher research productivity? This question is significant, as it has implications for our understanding of the drivers of research productivity, as well as the potential for innovative and entrepreneurial approaches to enhance academic performance.

This study makes several contributions to the existing literature. First, it provides insights into the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation and research productivity, which has been relatively unexplored in the context of academic research. Second, it examines the role of technological propensity, including the application of novel methods such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, in enhancing research productivity. Finally, this study contributes to our understanding of the challenges and opportunities faced by academics in developing countries, where resources may be limited and the need for innovative solutions is pressing. By exploring the intersection of entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and research productivity, this study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the factors influencing academic performance, as well as the potential for innovative and entrepreneurial approaches to drive research productivity in higher education.

## Methods

This study employed a quantitative research design to investigate the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity. A comprehensive review of the literature was conducted to inform the development of a survey instrument (Creswell, 2014). The survey was designed to capture data on the entrepreneurial orientation of academics, their propensity to apply novel technological methods, and their research productivity. A purposive sampling process was applied to select a large South African university as the site for data collection (Teddlie & Yu, 2007). This university was chosen due to its reputation for research excellence and its diverse range of academic disciplines.

The survey instrument was administered to a sample of academics across various faculties and departments within the university. The sampling frame consisted of all full-time academics employed by the university, totaling 1,200 individuals. A total of 500 surveys were distributed, and 320 responses were received, representing a response rate of 64%. However, after data cleaning and screening for missing values, 292 usable responses were obtained (Field, 2018). The respondents represented a range of academic disciplines, including natural sciences, social sciences, humanities, and engineering.

The survey instrument consisted of three main sections. The first section captured demographic data, including age, gender, academic rank, and discipline. The second section measured entrepreneurial orientation using a 12-item scale adapted from Miller (1983) and Covin and Wales (2012). This scale assessed the extent to which academics engaged in innovative, proactive, and risk-taking behaviors. The third section measured technological propensity using a 10-item scale developed by the researchers, which assessed the extent to which academics applied novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, in their research.

Research productivity was measured using a single item that asked respondents to report the number of publications they had authored in the past two years (Long, 1992). This measure has been widely used in previous studies as a proxy for research productivity (Fox, 1983). While it has its limitations, it provides a simple and straightforward indicator of research output.

Data analysis was conducted using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analysis, with research productivity as the dependent variable and entrepreneurial orientation and technological propensity as independent variables (Gujarati, 2014). The OLS model was specified as follows:

Research Productivity = β0 + β1(Entrepreneurial Orientation) + β2(Technological Propensity) + ε

Where β0 is the intercept, β1 and β2 are coefficients, and ε is the error term. The assumptions of OLS regression, including linearity, homoscedasticity, and normality of residuals, were tested and met (Field, 2018).

To test the robustness of the results, two further tests were applied. First, bootstrapping was used to estimate the coefficients and standard errors of the OLS model (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). This involved resampling the data with replacement 1,000 times and re-estimating the model for each resample. The results of the bootstrapping procedure were compared to the original OLS results to assess the stability of the estimates.

Second, negative binomial regression analysis was used to model the count data (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013). This was necessary because the research productivity variable was skewed and exhibited overdispersion, violating the assumptions of OLS regression. The negative binomial model was specified as follows:

Research Productivity ~ NegBin(μ, α)

Where μ is the mean, and α is the dispersion parameter. The results of the negative binomial regression analysis were compared to the OLS results to assess the sensitivity of the findings to the choice of model.

The data analysis was conducted using Stata 15 (StataCorp, 2017), and the results were interpreted in the context of the research questions and hypotheses. The findings of this study contribute to our understanding of the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity, and have implications for the development of strategies to enhance research productivity in higher education institutions.

## Results

The results of the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analysis are presented in Table 1, which shows the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity. The findings suggest that individuals with higher self-reported levels of entrepreneurial orientation (EO) tend to have higher levels of research productivity, as indicated by the positive and significant coefficient (β = 0.235, p < 0.01) (Cohen, 1988). This result is consistent with the argument that an entrepreneurial mindset can facilitate innovation and productivity in various contexts, including academia (Burgelman, 1983; Shane, 2000). The coefficient indicates that a one-unit increase in EO is associated with a 0.235-unit increase in research productivity, holding all other variables constant.

In contrast, the relationship between innovativeness and research productivity is not significant (β = 0.012, p > 0.10), suggesting that the ability to generate new ideas may not be a key driver of research productivity in this context. This finding is unexpected, given the emphasis on innovation in the entrepreneurship literature (Schumpeter, 1934; Drucker, 1985). However, it may be that innovativeness is not directly related to research productivity, but rather influences other factors, such as the ability to secure funding or collaborate with colleagues (Higgins, 2005).

The results also show that technological propensity is positively related to research productivity, although the coefficient is only marginally significant (β = 0.123, p < 0.10). This suggests that academics who are more prone to adopting novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, may have a slight advantage in terms of research productivity (Howell, 2015). However, the effect size is relatively small, indicating that technological propensity may not be a primary driver of research productivity.

To test the robustness of these results, we conducted two additional analyses: bootstrapping and negative binomial regression. The bootstrapping results, presented in Table 2, show that the coefficients for EO and technological propensity are consistent with the OLS results, although the standard errors are slightly larger (Efron, 1979). The negative binomial regression results, presented in Table 3, also show similar coefficients, although the model fit statistics indicate that the negative binomial model may be a better fit to the data (Cameron, 1998).

In terms of the control variables, the results show that age is negatively related to research productivity (β = -0.201, p < 0.05), suggesting that younger academics may be more productive than their older colleagues (Levin, 1992). This finding is consistent with the argument that younger academics may be more likely to take risks and pursue innovative research projects (Fuchs, 2011). The results also show that academic rank is positively related to research productivity (β = 0.351, p < 0.01), indicating that more senior academics tend to be more productive (Long, 1992).

Overall, the results suggest that entrepreneurial orientation is an important predictor of research productivity, while innovativeness and technological propensity may play a secondary role. These findings have implications for the development of training programs and policies aimed at promoting research productivity in higher education (Bess, 2000). For example, universities may consider offering courses or workshops on entrepreneurship and innovation, or providing resources and support for academics to pursue novel technological methods (Clarysse, 2011).

To further explore the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation and research productivity, we conducted a post-hoc analysis of the data. The results show that the relationship between EO and research productivity is strongest among academics in the natural sciences and engineering (β = 0.321, p < 0.01), and weakest among academics in the social sciences and humanities (β = 0.112, p > 0.10). This suggests that the benefits of an entrepreneurial orientation may be more pronounced in fields where innovation and commercialization are more prominent (Etzkowitz, 2003).

In addition, we found that the relationship between technological propensity and research productivity is stronger among academics who report higher levels of EO (β = 0.251, p < 0.05). This suggests that academics who are more entrepreneurial may be more likely to leverage novel technological methods to enhance their research productivity (Chesbrough, 2003). Overall, these post-hoc analysis results provide further insight into the complex relationships between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and research productivity, and highlight the need for further research in this area.

## Discussion and Conclusion

The findings of this study provide insight into the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity. The results suggest that individuals with higher self-reported levels of entrepreneurial orientation are more research productive, as evidenced by the positive and significant coefficient on the EO variable in the ordinary least squares regression model (β = 0.23, p < 0.01) (Cohen, 1988). This finding is consistent with the literature on entrepreneurial orientation, which suggests that individuals with higher levels of EO are more likely to engage in innovative and proactive behaviors (Miller, 1983; Covin & Wales, 2012). In the context of academic research, this may manifest as a greater willingness to explore new research questions, collaborate with colleagues from diverse disciplines, and seek out external funding opportunities (Bae & Kattan, 2012).

Interestingly, the results of this study do not support a significant relationship between innovativeness and academic research productivity. This finding is somewhat surprising, given the emphasis on innovation in the entrepreneurial orientation literature (Schumpeter, 1934). One possible explanation for this result is that innovativeness, while important for entrepreneurial success in other contexts, may not be as critical in the academic research environment. As noted by Kuhn (1962), academic research is often conducted within established paradigms, which may limit the scope for innovative thinking. Alternatively, it is possible that the measure of innovativeness used in this study did not capture the full range of innovative behaviors engaged in by academics (Kirton, 1976).

The findings of this study also highlight the potential for novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, to contribute to academic research productivity. While the results do not support a significant relationship between technological propensity and research productivity, the descriptive statistics suggest that these methods are currently underutilized in the academic context (mean = 1.4, SD = 0.8). This is consistent with the literature on the adoption of new technologies, which suggests that academics may be slow to adopt new methods due to a range of barriers, including lack of awareness, lack of training, and concerns about intellectual property (Rogers, 2003). Given the potential benefits of these methods, including increased funding opportunities and enhanced collaboration (Howell, 2013), it is surprising that they are not more widely used.

The conclusions of this study have important implications for theory and practice. From a theoretical perspective, the findings suggest that further synthesis between educational and entrepreneurship theory may be useful for understanding the factors that contribute to academic research productivity (Shane & Venkataraman, 2000). This may involve exploring the ways in which entrepreneurial orientation and technological propensity interact to influence research outcomes, as well as the role of other factors, such as social capital and institutional support (Bourdieu, 1986). From a practical perspective, the findings suggest that universities and other research institutions may be able to improve research productivity by providing training and support for academics in areas such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D (Wright, 2014). This may involve partnering with industry and other external organizations to provide access to new technologies and funding opportunities (Etzkowitz, 2003).

There are several limitations to this study that should be noted. First, the study is based on a sample of academics from a single university, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other contexts (Tashakkori & Teddlie, 2010). Second, the study relies on self-reported measures of entrepreneurial orientation and technological propensity, which may be subject to bias and social desirability effects (Podsakoff & Organ, 1986). Finally, the study does not account for other factors that may influence research productivity, such as institutional support and social capital (Bourdieu, 1986). Future research should seek to address these limitations by using more diverse samples, objective measures of entrepreneurial orientation and technological propensity, and controlling for other factors that may influence research outcomes.

In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity. The findings suggest that individuals with higher levels of entrepreneurial orientation are more research productive, and that novel technological methods such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D may be underutilized in the academic context. Further research is needed to explore the ways in which these factors interact to influence research outcomes, as well as the role of other factors, such as social capital and institutional support. By addressing these questions, researchers and practitioners may be able to identify new strategies for improving academic research productivity, and contributing to the development of new knowledge and innovations that address societally important problems (Merton, 1973).

## Introduction

The prevalence of obesity has increased significantly over the past few decades, affecting millions of people worldwide (Hruby and Hu, 2015). As a result, the number of individuals undergoing weight loss procedures, either through surgical or non-surgical methods, has also increased substantially (Buchwald et al., 2004). However, significant weight loss is often accompanied by excess skin laxity and redundancy, which can lead to a range of physical and psychological problems, including limited mobility, skin irritation, and decreased self-esteem (Kitzinger, 2011). Body-contouring surgery, which includes procedures such as abdominoplasty, mammoplasty, and brachioplasty, offers a solution to these problems by removing excess skin and reshaping the body (Nemerofsky et al., 2012).

Despite the growing popularity of body-contouring surgery after weight loss, there is a significant gap in our understanding of the psychosocial impact of these procedures on patients (Sarwer et al., 2010). While several studies have investigated the physical benefits of body-contouring surgery, including improved mobility and reduced skin irritation (Shermak et al., 2010), few have examined the psychological and social effects of these procedures (Sarwer et al., 2011). This is an important omission, as the psychological and social benefits of body-contouring surgery are likely to be just as significant as the physical benefits, if not more so (Sarwer et al., 2012).

One of the key psychological benefits of body-contouring surgery is the improvement in self-esteem and body image (Brown et al., 2013). Excess skin laxity and redundancy can lead to feelings of self-consciousness and embarrassment, which can negatively impact an individual's self-esteem and overall quality of life (Gilmartin, 2015). By removing excess skin and reshaping the body, body-contouring surgery can help to improve an individual's self-esteem and body image, leading to a more positive and confident self-perception (Stevens et al., 2013). Additionally, body-contouring surgery can also improve an individual's social interactions and relationships, as they become more confident in their appearance and more willing to engage in social activities (Klassen et al., 2012).

However, despite these potential benefits, there is a need for further research into the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery after weight loss. Many of the existing studies in this area are limited by small sample sizes, inadequate control groups, and short follow-up periods (Sarwer et al., 2010). Furthermore, few studies have used validated psychosocial measures to assess the outcomes of body-contouring surgery, which can make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of these procedures (Nemerofsky et al., 2012).

The research question guiding this study is: What are the psychosocial effects of body-contouring surgery on patients after weight loss? Specifically, we aim to investigate the impact of body-contouring surgery on the quality of life, self-esteem, and social interactions of patients who have undergone significant weight loss. We also aim to examine the satisfaction rates of patients with different types of body-contouring procedures, including abdominoplasty, mammoplasty, and brachioplasty. By addressing these research questions, this study aims to contribute to the existing literature on the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery after weight loss, and to provide valuable insights for clinicians and patients considering these procedures.

The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive examination of the psychosocial effects of body-contouring surgery on patients after weight loss, using a validated questionnaire and a sample of patients with a minimum follow-up period of 6 months. Secondly, it examines the satisfaction rates of patients with different types of body-contouring procedures, which can help to inform clinical decision-making and patient counseling. Finally, it highlights the importance of considering the psychosocial outcomes of body-contouring surgery, in addition to the physical outcomes, in order to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the benefits and risks of these procedures. By examining the psychosocial effects of body-contouring surgery, this study aims to provide a more nuanced and detailed understanding of the outcomes of these procedures, and to contribute to the development of more effective and patient-centered treatment approaches.

## Methods

This cross-sectional study was designed to assess the psychosocial impact of body-contouring surgery on patients after weight loss. The study population consisted of patients who had undergone body-contouring surgery at a plastic surgery clinic. The inclusion criteria were patients who had lost 20 kg or less before the surgery and were at least 6 months postoperative (Shiffman, 1992). A total of 43 patients met the inclusion criteria and were recruited for the study. The sample size was determined based on a power analysis, which indicated that a minimum of 30 patients would be required to detect a significant difference in psychosocial outcomes (Cohen, 1988).

Data were collected during a single visit to the plastic surgery clinic. A specifically designed questionnaire was developed in collaboration with the psychiatric department for our research (Kessler et al., 2002). The questionnaire was designed to assess the patients' psychosocial status before and after surgery, including quality of life, social life, job performance, sexual activity, and symptoms of depression. The questionnaire consisted of 30 items, including 10 items related to quality of life, 5 items related to social life, 5 items related to job performance, 5 items related to sexual activity, and 5 items related to symptoms of depression. The items were scored on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

The questionnaire was pilot-tested on a sample of 10 patients who had undergone body-contouring surgery to ensure its validity and reliability (DeVellis, 2003). The pilot testing revealed that the questionnaire had good internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of 0.85. The questionnaire was also found to have good test-retest reliability, with a correlation coefficient of 0.80.

The data were analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 20(IBM Corp, 2011). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic characteristics of the patients, including age, sex, and type of surgery. The mean and standard deviation were used to describe continuous variables, while frequencies and percentages were used to describe categorical variables. Inferential statistics were used to compare the psychosocial outcomes before and after surgery. Paired t-tests were used to compare the means of continuous variables, while McNemar's test was used to compare the proportions of categorical variables (Fleiss, 1981).
