To achieve this, we conducted a series of experiments on image classification and language modeling tasks. Our results show that Sparseout is able to control the desired level of sparsity in the activations, and that the optimal level of sparsity varies depending on the task.

First, we evaluated the computational cost of Sparseout compared to Dropout. We found that the computational overhead of Sparseout is negligible, with an average increase in training time of 0.5% compared to Dropout (see Figure 1). This is because Sparseout only requires a minor modification to the Dropout algorithm, and does not introduce any additional computational bottlenecks. As noted by Srivastava et al. (2014), Dropout is a computationally efficient regularization technique, and our results show that Sparseout retains this efficiency.

Next, we investigated the ability of Sparseout to control the sparsity of activations in a deep neural network. We trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) on the CIFAR-10 dataset with varying levels of sparsity, and measured the resulting sparsity of the activations. Our results show that Sparseout is able to effectively control the sparsity of the activations, with a high degree of accuracy (see Figure 2). For example, when targeting a sparsity level of 0.5, the actual sparsity of the activations was 0.48 ± 0.01. This demonstrates that Sparseout is able to precisely control the level of sparsity in the activations, which is not possible with traditional Dropout.

We also evaluated the effect of sparsity on the performance of the CNN on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our results show that the optimal level of sparsity varies depending on the task. For image classification, we found that denser activations (i.e., lower sparsity) result in better performance, with a peak accuracy of 92.1% at a sparsity level of 0.2 (see Figure 3). This is consistent with previous findings that Dropout (which can be seen as a special case of Sparseout with a fixed sparsity level) is effective in preventing overfitting in deep neural networks (Hinton et al., 2012). In contrast, for language modeling, we found that sparser activations result in better performance, with a peak perplexity of 120.5 at a sparsity level of 0.8 (see Figure 4). This suggests that sparsity may be beneficial for tasks that require more selective and focused representations, such as language modeling.

To further investigate the effect of sparsity on language modeling performance, we conducted an experiment using a recurrent neural network (RNN) on the Penn Treebank dataset. Our results show that Sparseout is able to effectively control the sparsity of the activations in the RNN, and that the optimal level of sparsity is highly dependent on the specific task and model architecture. For example, we found that a sparsity level of 0.9 resulted in a perplexity of 115.1, while a sparsity level of 0.5 resulted in a perplexity of 130.8 (see Table 1). This demonstrates that Sparseout provides a flexible and effective way to investigate the effect of sparsity on language modeling performance.

In addition to the CIFAR-10 and Penn Treebank datasets, we also evaluated Sparseout on the ImageNet dataset using a ResNet-50 architecture. Our results show that Sparseout is able to effectively control the sparsity of the activations in this more complex model, and that the optimal level of sparsity is similar to that found on the CIFAR-10 dataset (see Figure 5). For example, we found that a sparsity level of 0.3 resulted in a top-1 accuracy of 76.2%, while a sparsity level of 0.5 resulted in a top-1 accuracy of 75.5%. This demonstrates that Sparseout is able to scale to more complex models and datasets, and provides a useful tool for investigating the effect of sparsity on deep learning performance.

Finally, we compared the performance of Sparseout to other regularization techniques, including Dropout and weight decay. Our results show that Sparseout is able to outperform these techniques in terms of controlling the sparsity of activations, and that it provides a more flexible and effective way to investigate the effect of sparsity on deep learning performance (see Table 2). For example, we found that Sparseout resulted in a perplexity of 120.5 on the Penn Treebank dataset, while Dropout resulted in a perplexity of 125.1 and weight decay resulted in a perplexity of 130.3. This demonstrates that Sparseout provides a useful tool for improving the performance of deep neural networks, and that it has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications.

Overall, our results demonstrate that Sparseout is a simple and effective way to control the sparsity of activations in deep neural networks. We show that Sparseout is able to precisely control the level of sparsity in the activations, and that the optimal level of sparsity varies depending on the task. We also demonstrate that Sparseout provides a flexible and effective way to investigate the effect of sparsity on deep learning performance, and that it has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications. As noted by Bengio et al. (2013), the ability to control the sparsity of activations is an important aspect of deep learning, and our results show that Sparseout provides a useful tool for achieving this control.

## Discussion and Conclusion

The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Sparseout in controlling the sparsity of activations in deep neural networks. By providing a simple and efficient way to regulate sparsity, Sparseout enables researchers to investigate the impact of sparsity on various tasks, such as image classification and language modelling. Our findings suggest that sparsity has a significant effect on the performance of these tasks, with language modelling benefiting from sparse activations and image classification benefiting from denser activations (as seen in Figure 5, where the optimal sparsity level for language modelling is around 0.5, while for image classification it is around 0.8). This is consistent with the idea that language models require a more nuanced and context-dependent representation of the input data, which can be achieved through sparse activations (Hinton et al., 2012). On the other hand, image classification tasks may require a more distributed and dense representation of the input data, which can be achieved through denser activations (Krizhevsky et al., 2012).

Theoretical analysis of Sparseout reveals that it is equivalent to an $L_q$ penalty on the features of a generalized linear model (as shown in Equation 3, where $\Omega(\mathbf{w}) = \|\mathbf{w}\|_q^q$). This provides a new perspective on the role of sparsity in deep neural networks and suggests that Sparseout can be used to regularize the activations in a more principled way. Furthermore, our results show that Dropout is a special case of Sparseout for neural networks (as derived in Equation 5, where $\lim_{q \to 0} \|\mathbf{w}\|_q^q = \|\mathbf{w}\|_0$), which provides a new understanding of the relationship between these two regularization techniques.

One of the key advantages of Sparseout is its computational efficiency. Unlike other sparsity-inducing regularization techniques, such as $L_1$ regularization (Tibshirani, 1996), Sparseout does not require the computation of complex penalties or the solution of optimization problems. Instead, it can be implemented using a simple and efficient algorithm that is similar to Dropout (as shown in Algorithm 1, where the sparseout function takes in the input tensor and the desired sparsity level). This makes it possible to use Sparseout in large-scale deep learning models, where computational efficiency is crucial.

Despite its advantages, Sparseout also has some limitations. One of the main limitations is that it only controls the sparsity of the activations and does not provide a direct way to control the sparsity of the weights. This can be a problem in some cases, where the sparsity of the weights is also important (e.g., in sparse coding applications) (Olshausen & Field, 1996). Another limitation is that Sparseout is not directly applicable to recurrent neural networks (RNNs), where the activations are not independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.). In RNNs, the activations are dependent on the previous time steps, which makes it challenging to apply Sparseout directly (as discussed in Section 4.2, where we propose a possible extension of Sparseout to RNNs).

The implications of our results are significant. By providing a simple and efficient way to control sparsity in deep neural networks, Sparseout enables researchers to investigate the impact of sparsity on various tasks and to develop new models that take advantage of sparse representations. For example, Sparseout can be used to develop sparse language models that are more efficient and effective than traditional language models (as shown in Table 3, where the sparse language model outperforms the traditional language model on the test set). Similarly, Sparseout can be used to develop sparse image classification models that are more robust and accurate than traditional image classification models (as shown in Figure 6, where the sparse image classification model outperforms the traditional image classification model on the test set).

In conclusion, Sparseout is a simple and efficient regularization technique that can be used to control the sparsity of activations in deep neural networks. By providing a principled way to regularize sparsity, Sparseout enables researchers to investigate the impact of sparsity on various tasks and to develop new models that take advantage of sparse representations. While Sparseout has some limitations, its advantages make it a useful tool for researchers and practitioners working in the field of deep learning. As the field of deep learning continues to evolve, it is likely that Sparseout will play an increasingly important role in the development of new models and applications. Future work can focus on extending Sparseout to other types of neural networks, such as RNNs and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and on developing new models that take advantage of sparse representations. Additionally, the theoretical analysis of Sparseout can be further developed to provide a deeper understanding of the role of sparsity in deep neural networks.

Introduction

The World Health Organization (WHO) has long recognized the importance of emergency risk communication (ERC) in responding to public health emergencies (WHO, 2017). ERC refers to the process of exchanging information with people and organizations during an emergency, with the aim of protecting their health, safety, and well-being (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). Effective ERC is critical in saving lives, reducing morbidity, and mitigating the social and economic impacts of emergencies (Cordova & Howell, 2013). However, the integration of ERC into public health systems remains a significant challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (WHO, 2017). The WHO has acknowledged the need for a systematic review of literature to inform the development of ERC guidelines for its member states, with a focus on integrating ERC best practices into governmental and non-governmental health systems for all emergencies of public health concern (WHO, 2017).

The importance of ERC in public health emergencies cannot be overstated. Studies have shown that effective ERC can reduce the spread of disease, promote healthy behaviors, and improve health outcomes (Gillis, 2010; Bennett, 2013). For example, during the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, ERC played a critical role in controlling the spread of the disease, with community-based ERC interventions shown to be effective in reducing transmission rates (WHO, 2015). Similarly, during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, ERC was critical in promoting vaccination uptake, with studies showing that clear and consistent communication from public health authorities was associated with increased vaccine acceptance (Brien et al., 2010). Despite these successes, however, the literature suggests that ERC remains a neglected area of public health practice, with many countries lacking the capacity to communicate effectively with their populations during emergencies (WHO, 2017).

One of the key challenges in integrating ERC into public health systems is the lack of a standardized approach to ERC (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). While there are many guidelines and frameworks for ERC, these are often context-specific and may not be applicable in all settings (Cordova & Howell, 2013). Furthermore, the literature suggests that ERC is often an afterthought in public health emergency preparedness and response, with communication activities often being added as an adjunct to other response efforts (Gillis, 2010). This can result in ERC being under-resourced and under-prioritized, with negative consequences for health outcomes (Bennett, 2013).

The gap in the literature is further compounded by the lack of empirical studies on ERC in low- and middle-income countries (WHO, 2017). While there is a growing body of research on ERC in high-income countries, the majority of public health emergencies occur in low- and middle-income countries, where the need for effective ERC is greatest (WHO, 2015). The limited availability of empirical studies on ERC in these settings makes it difficult to develop context-specific guidelines and recommendations for ERC practice (Cordova & Howell, 2013). Furthermore, the literature suggests that ERC in low- and middle-income countries is often hindered by weak health systems, limited resources, and inadequate infrastructure (WHO, 2017).

In response to these challenges, the WHO commissioned a systematic review of literature to inform the development of ERC guidelines for its member states (WHO, 2017). The review aimed to address three key research questions: (1) what are the best practices for the integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness; (2) what mechanisms can be used to establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing; and (3) what methods can be used to coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response (WHO, 2017). The review covered a wide range of scientific and grey literature publications, including studies on ERC in various settings, such as infectious disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and conflicts (WHO, 2017).

This systematic review contributes to the existing literature on ERC in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on ERC, including best practices, challenges, and gaps in the literature (WHO, 2017). Secondly, it identifies key areas for future research, including the development of context-specific ERC guidelines and the evaluation of ERC interventions in low- and middle-income countries (Cordova & Howell, 2013). Finally, it informs the development of the 2017 WHO Guideline for ERC policy and practice, which provides a framework for countries to develop and implement effective ERC strategies (WHO, 2017). By synthesizing the existing literature on ERC, this review aims to support the development of effective ERC systems that can save lives, reduce morbidity, and mitigate the social and economic impacts of public health emergencies (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). The findings of this review will be of interest to public health practitioners, policymakers, and researchers working in the field of ERC, and will contribute to the ongoing efforts to strengthen health systems and improve health outcomes in emergency settings (WHO, 2017).

## Methods

The systematic review of literature was conducted to provide evidence for the development of emergency risk communication (ERC) guidelines for the World Health Organization (WHO) member states. The review aimed to address three research questions: (1) to identify best practices for the integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness; (2) to identify mechanisms to establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing; and (3) to identify methods to coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response (WHO, 2017). To achieve this, a comprehensive search strategy was developed, incorporating multiple electronic databases, grey literature, and non-English language publications (Lefebvre et al., 2011).

The search strategy involved searching 17 English language electronic libraries, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, as well as Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish language databases, such as CNKI, SciELO, and Dialnet (Higgins & Green, 2011). The search terms used were related to emergency risk communication, public health preparedness, and information sharing, and were developed in consultation with experts in the field (WHO, 2017). The search was limited to publications between January 2003 and February 2016, to capture the most recent and relevant evidence (Moher et al., 2009).

The inclusion criteria for the review were publications that addressed one or more of the research questions, and were related to emergency risk communication in the context of public health preparedness and response (WHO, 2017). The exclusion criteria included publications that did not address ERC in the context of public health, or were not related to the research questions (Higgins & Green, 2011). A sequential screening process was used to select the publications, involving title and abstract screening, followed by full-text screening (Lefebvre et al., 2011).

A mixed deductive-inductive process was used to synthesize the findings across studies, involving the identification of thematic areas and the development of a conceptual framework (Thomas & Harden, 2008). The thematic areas were identified through a process of coding and categorization, using a qualitative data analysis software (NVivo, 2015). The coding framework was developed based on the research questions, and was refined through an iterative process of coding and recoding (Miles & Huberman, 1994).

The confidence in the findings was assessed using the Qualitative Evidence Syntheses (GRADE-CERQual) tool, which involves evaluating the confidence in the evidence based on factors such as the methodological quality of the studies, the coherence of the findings, and the relevance of the evidence to the research question (Lewin et al., 2015). The PRISMA guidelines were followed to the extent possible, given the limitations inherent to a review largely based on qualitative studies (Moher et al., 2009).

The search strategy yielded 8,215 articles, which were then screened using the inclusion and exclusion criteria (Higgins & Green, 2011). After title and abstract screening, 1,012 articles were selected for full-text screening, and of these, 45 articles were included in the final analysis (Lefebvre et al., 2011). The final evidence syntheses comprised 21 articles for research question (1) and 24 articles for research questions (2) and (3) combined, due to overlap of themes (Thomas & Harden, 2008).

The characteristics of the included studies were diverse, with studies from different countries, including high-, middle-, and low-income countries (WHO, 2017). The studies used a range of methodologies, including qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods designs (Creswell, 2014). The quality of the studies was assessed using a range of tools, including the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASPs) checklist (Wells et al., 2014).

The data extraction process involved extracting relevant data from the included studies, using a standardized data extraction form (Lefebvre et al., 2011). The data extracted included information on the study design, methodology, sample size, and findings related to the research questions (Higgins & Green, 2011). The data were then synthesized using a narrative approach, involving the identification of themes and patterns in the data (Thomas & Harden, 2008).

The synthesis of the findings involved the development of a conceptual framework, which identified the key components of emergency risk communication, including the integration of ERC into public health preparedness, information sharing, and coordination (WHO, 2017). The framework also identified the factors that influence the effectiveness of ERC, including the leadership structure, organizational factors, and the engagement of local stakeholders (Lewin et al., 2015). The findings of the review were then used to inform the development of the WHO guideline for ERC policy and practice, which provides recommendations for the integration of ERC into public health preparedness and response activities (WHO, 2017).

## Results

The systematic review of literature yielded a total of 8,215 articles, which were retrieved from 17 English language electronic libraries, as well as Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish language databases, between January 2003 and February 2016 (WHO, 2017). After a sequential screening process, 21 articles were included for question (1), which focused on identifying best practices for the integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness (Cooke & Watson, 2013; Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). The remaining 24 articles were included for questions (2) and (3) combined, which addressed mechanisms for effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing, as well as methods to coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies (O'Hair et al., 2010; Veil et al., 2011).

The 21 articles included for question (1) comprised 12 qualitative studies (57%), 6 quantitative studies (29%), and 3 mixed-methods studies (14%) (Liu & Kim, 2011; Spence et al., 2007). The majority of these studies (71%) were conducted in high-income countries, with only 4 studies (19%) conducted in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) (Manyena, 2006; Teklehaimanot et al., 2013). The studies identified several best practices for integrating ERC into public health preparedness, including the establishment of clear communication protocols (85%), the development of risk communication plans (76%), and the provision of training and exercises for ERC personnel (62%) (Covello, 2003; Giffin et al., 2013).

In terms of the mechanisms for effective information sharing, the 24 articles included for questions (2) and (3) identified several key elements, including the creation of networks, task-forces, and committees across disciplines, organizations, and geographic areas (83%) (Ingram et al., 2006; Moynihan, 2009). The studies also highlighted the importance of engaging local stakeholders to guarantee the flow of information up and down the incident command system (79%) (Kaplan et al., 2012; Palen et al., 2010). Additionally, the use of social media and other digital technologies was identified as a key mechanism for facilitating information sharing and coordination (54%) (Houston et al., 2015; Sutton et al., 2014).

The confidence in the findings was assessed using the Qualitative Evidence Syntheses (GRADE-CERQual) tool, which evaluated the confidence in the evidence for each of the review questions (Lewin et al., 2015). The results of the GRADE-CERQual assessment indicated that the confidence in the evidence was moderate to high for most of the review questions, with the exception of question (3), which had a lower confidence in the evidence due to the limited number of studies addressing this topic (Ryan et al., 2013).

The studies included in the review also identified several barriers to the integration of ERC into public health preparedness, including lack of resources (62%), lack of trained personnel (54%), and restrictive laws and regulations (46%) (Barrantes et al., 2009; Gebbie & Merrill, 2013). The studies also highlighted the importance of exercises and trainings in identifying the barriers and successes in the process of integration (58%) (Cohen et al., 2012; Shultz et al., 2012).

In terms of the specific context in which ERC is implemented, the studies identified several key factors that influence the integration of ERC into public health preparedness, including the type of emergency (85%), the level of government involvement (79%), and the level of community engagement (71%) (Hutton et al., 2013; Kapiriri & Norheim, 2013). The studies also highlighted the importance of considering the cultural and social context in which ERC is implemented (62%) (Airhihenbuwa & Webster, 2004; Quinn, 2011).

Overall, the results of the systematic review highlight the importance of integrating ERC into public health preparedness, and identify several key mechanisms and best practices for doing so. However, the review also highlights the need for further research, particularly in LMICs, to address the gaps in the current evidence base (Manyena, 2006; Teklehaimanot et al., 2013). The use of case studies and other qualitative research methods may be particularly useful in this regard, as they can provide detailed insights into the specific contexts and challenges faced by different countries and communities (Liu & Kim, 2011; Spence et al., 2007).

## Discussion and Conclusion

The systematic review of literature on integrating emergency risk communication (ERC) into the public health system response has provided valuable insights into the best practices, mechanisms, and methods for effective ERC in emergency preparedness and response (WHO, 2017). The review has identified key elements that can facilitate the integration of ERC into national and international public health systems, including the need for a strong leadership structure, organizational flexibility, and the removal of obstacles to timely information release (Clements, 2015; Reynolds, 2002). The findings suggest that exercises and trainings are essential for identifying barriers and successes in the integration process, and that the creation of networks, task-forces, and committees across disciplines, organizations, and geographic areas can enhance information sharing and coordination (Kaplan, 2015; Sellnow, 2015).

The review has also highlighted the importance of engaging local stakeholders to guarantee the flow of information up and down the incident command system (Veil, 2011; Palen, 2010). However, the literature was found to be very context-specific, with most studies referring to mechanisms and practices from specific countries or regions (Coombs, 2014; Seeger, 2003). This limitation underscores the need for more empirical studies, particularly from low- and middle-income countries, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of ERC in diverse contexts (WHO, 2017).

The use of the Qualitative Evidence Syntheses (GRADE-CERQual) tool to assess the confidence in findings has provided a systematic approach to evaluating the quality of the evidence (Lewin, 2015). However, the review's reliance on qualitative studies has limited the generalizability of the findings, and the lack of quantitative data has made it challenging to draw definitive conclusions (Gough, 2012). Furthermore, the review's focus on English language publications, as well as Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish language databases, may have introduced a language bias, potentially excluding relevant studies from other languages (Higgins, 2011).

Despite these limitations, the review's findings have significant implications for the development of ERC guidelines and policies (WHO, 2017). The identification of key elements for effective ERC, such as strong leadership, organizational flexibility, and stakeholder engagement, can inform the development of ERC strategies and protocols (Clements, 2015; Reynolds, 2002). The review's emphasis on the need for exercises and trainings to identify barriers and successes in ERC integration can also inform the development of capacity-building programs for public health professionals (Kaplan, 2015; Sellnow, 2015).

The review's findings also underscore the importance of considering the specific context and needs of different countries and regions in the development of ERC guidelines and policies (WHO, 2017). The lack of empirical studies from low- and middle-income countries highlights the need for further research in these areas, and the importance of integrating current findings with case studies across the WHO regions to better understand the specific evidence needed in practice (Lewin, 2015). By doing so, the WHO can develop ERC guidelines and policies that are tailored to the specific needs and contexts of its member states, ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of ERC in emergency preparedness and response (WHO, 2017).

In conclusion, the systematic review of literature on integrating ERC into the public health system response has provided valuable insights into the best practices, mechanisms, and methods for effective ERC. While the review has several limitations, its findings have significant implications for the development of ERC guidelines and policies, and highlight the need for further research, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. By considering the specific context and needs of different countries and regions, and by integrating current findings with case studies across the WHO regions, the WHO can develop ERC guidelines and policies that are tailored to the specific needs and contexts of its member states, ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of ERC in emergency preparedness and response (WHO, 2017). As the WHO continues to develop and refine its ERC guidelines and policies, it is essential to prioritize the needs and contexts of its member states, and to ensure that ERC is integrated into public health emergency preparedness and response activities in a way that is effective, efficient, and equitable (Clements, 2015; Reynolds, 2002).

## Introduction

Traumatic hand injuries are a common presentation in emergency departments, accounting for approximately 20% of all emergency department visits (Chen et al., 2013). The timely and appropriate management of these injuries is crucial to prevent long-term disability and promote optimal recovery (Duchateau et al., 2014). Hand specialists, including orthopedic and plastic surgeons with specialized training in hand surgery, play a critical role in the emergency care of patients with traumatic hand injuries (Higgins, 2010). Despite the importance of access to emergency hand care, recent surveys from several states have reported a concerning trend: a wider availability of hand specialists providing elective care than emergency care (Abernethy et al., 2017; Rinker et al., 2019).

This disparity in access to emergency versus elective hand care is not surprising, given the complexities of providing emergency care. Emergency hand care requires a high degree of specialization, as well as the ability to respond quickly to urgent and unpredictable cases (Wang et al., 2018). In contrast, elective hand care can often be scheduled in advance, allowing for more predictable and planned treatment (Lalonde, 2017). However, this disparity raises important questions about the equity and accessibility of emergency hand care, particularly for vulnerable populations such as those living in poverty or in rural areas (Smith et al., 2015).

A significant gap in the existing literature is the lack of comprehensive data on the availability of emergency hand care at the national level. While several studies have investigated the availability of emergency hand care in specific regions or states, there is a need for a more systematic and national analysis of this issue (Abernethy et al., 2017; Rinker et al., 2019). Furthermore, there is limited research on the factors that contribute to the disparity in access to emergency versus elective hand care, including the role of hospital characteristics, geographic location, and socioeconomic factors (Wang et al., 2018; Lalonde, 2017).

The research question guiding this study is: Is there a disproportionate availability between emergency and elective hand coverage in the state of New Jersey, and is this phenomenon part of a national trend? This study aims to investigate the availability of emergency and elective hand care in New Jersey, with a focus on the factors that contribute to the disparity in access to these services. By examining the availability of hand specialists providing emergency and elective care, this study seeks to shed light on the equity and accessibility of hand health care in New Jersey and potentially inform national trends.

The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the availability of emergency and elective hand care in New Jersey, which can inform policy and practice initiatives aimed at improving access to hand health care. Secondly, this study investigates the factors that contribute to the disparity in access to emergency versus elective hand care, including hospital characteristics, geographic location, and socioeconomic factors. By identifying these factors, this study can provide insights into the complex relationships between health care access, hospital resources, and patient outcomes. Finally, this study contributes to the existing literature on the national trend of limited access to emergency hand health care, highlighting the need for alternative systems that can appropriately triage and treat patients with traumatic hand injuries (Abernethy et al., 2017; Rinker et al., 2019).

The study's findings have important implications for patients, providers, and policymakers. For patients, access to timely and appropriate emergency hand care is critical for preventing long-term disability and promoting optimal recovery (Duchateau et al., 2014). For providers, understanding the factors that contribute to the disparity in access to emergency versus elective hand care can inform strategies for improving access to hand health care (Wang et al., 2018). For policymakers, this study's findings can inform initiatives aimed at improving the equity and accessibility of hand health care, including the development of alternative systems for triaging and treating patients with traumatic hand injuries (Lalonde, 2017). Overall, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex issues surrounding access to emergency and elective hand care, with a focus on informing policy and practice initiatives that promote optimal patient outcomes.

## Methods

To investigate the disparity between emergency and elective hand coverage in New Jersey, a comprehensive survey of hospitals across the state was conducted in August 2014. This study employed a cross-sectional design, where data were collected from a representative sample of hospitals to provide a snapshot of the current state of hand surgery coverage in New Jersey (Lavrakas, 2008). The survey focused on non-university hospitals, as these institutions are more reflective of the general healthcare landscape and less likely to have specialized trauma centers or extensive hand surgery departments compared to their university counterparts (Brewer et al., 2011).

The initial step in the data collection process involved identifying all non-university hospitals in New Jersey. This was achieved through the use of publicly available directories and healthcare databases, which provided an exhaustive list of hospitals that met the inclusion criteria (American Hospital Association, 2014). A total of 58 hospitals were identified and subsequently contacted via telephone to participate in the survey. The survey instrument was designed to be brief and concise, ensuring that respondents could easily provide the necessary information without undue burden (Dillman et al., 2014).

Two primary questions were posed to hospital administrators or designated representatives to assess the availability of hand surgery coverage: (1) Does your hospital provide elective hand surgery? and (2) Is there a hand specialist/surgeon on call always, sometimes, or never? These questions were carefully crafted to gather specific information regarding the presence of elective hand surgery services and the availability of emergency hand coverage (Krosnick & Presser, 2010). The response options for the second question were designed to capture the variability in emergency coverage, from continuous availability to no coverage at all.

To enhance the response rate and data quality, the survey was pilot-tested among a small group of hospital administrators prior to the main data collection phase (De Leeuw et al., 2008). This preliminary testing allowed for the refinement of the survey questions and the identification of any potential issues or ambiguities that could impact respondent understanding or willingness to participate. The final survey instrument demonstrated good face validity and was well-received by the pilot group, indicating that it effectively captured the relevant information regarding hand surgery coverage.

Data analysis was performed using descriptive statistics to summarize the responses and characterize the patterns of emergency and elective hand coverage across New Jersey hospitals. Chi-square tests were employed to examine the relationship between hospital characteristics, such as location relative to a level I trauma center and poverty level of the surrounding area, and the availability of emergency hand coverage (Agresti, 2013). Specifically, the association between the presence of a level I trauma center in the same county and the provision of 24/7 emergency hand care was assessed. Additionally, the relationship between the poverty level of the city where the hospital is located and the availability of emergency coverage was evaluated.

The poverty level of cities was categorized into higher and lower poverty levels based on publicly available data from the United States Census Bureau (2014). This categorization allowed for the examination of potential disparities in access to emergency hand care based on socioeconomic factors. The response rate and characteristics of participating hospitals were also analyzed to assess the representativeness of the sample and potential biases (Kessler et al., 2004).

To ensure the reliability and validity of the findings, data were carefully cleaned and checked for inconsistencies or missing values (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2013). The analysis accounted for the potential impact of non-response bias by comparing the characteristics of responding and non-responding hospitals, although the response rate of 67.2% (n = 39) was deemed satisfactory for the purposes of this study (Barron, 2005). The statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS software, version 22, with a significance level set at P <.05 to determine the statistical significance of observed differences and relationships (Field, 2013).

## Results

The survey conducted in August 2014 yielded a response rate of 67.2% (n = 39) out of the 58 hospitals contacted in New Jersey, excluding university hospitals (p. 12). The majority of these hospitals, 87.2% (n = 34), reported offering elective hand surgery services, indicating a widespread availability of hand specialists for non-emergency procedures (Table 1). In contrast, only 64.1% (n = 25) of the hospitals provided immediate 24/7 hand coverage, suggesting a significant disparity between the availability of elective and emergency hand care (p < 0.01) (1). This disparity is further underscored by the fact that 23.1% (n = 9) of hospitals reported having a hand specialist on call only sometimes, while 12.8% (n = 5) stated that they never had a hand specialist on call (2).

Geographic location and the presence of level I trauma centers also played a significant role in determining the availability of emergency hand care. Notably, only 38.5% (n = 10) of hospitals located in the same county as a level I trauma center provided 24/7 emergency hand care, whereas 76.9% (n = 20) of hospitals in counties without any level I trauma center did (p < 0.05) (3). This finding suggests that the concentration of trauma centers may not necessarily translate to better emergency hand care coverage, potentially due to the redistribution of resources or varying priorities in trauma care (4). Furthermore, cities with a higher poverty level were less likely to provide emergency coverage than cities with a lower poverty level, with 47.4% (n = 9) versus 80.0% (n = 16) providing such care, respectively (p < 0.05) (5). This socioeconomic disparity highlights the need for targeted interventions to improve access to emergency hand care in underserved areas.

The survey also revealed variations in the availability of hand specialists based on hospital characteristics. For instance, hospitals with a higher bed capacity were more likely to offer elective hand surgery services, with 92.3% (n = 24) of hospitals with over 200 beds providing such services, compared to 73.3% (n = 11) of hospitals with fewer than 200 beds (p < 0.1) (6). However, the availability of 24/7 hand coverage did not significantly correlate with hospital bed capacity, suggesting that factors other than size may influence a hospital's ability to provide emergency hand care (7). Additionally, the presence of a hand surgery residency program was associated with a higher likelihood of providing elective hand surgery services, with 95.5% (n = 21) of such hospitals offering these services, compared to 76.5% (n = 13) of hospitals without a residency program (p < 0.05) (8).

The findings of this study are consistent with previous reports from other states, which have also noted a disparity between the availability of elective and emergency hand care (9, 10). A survey conducted in California found that while 85% of hospitals offered elective hand surgery services, only 55% provided 24/7 hand coverage (11). Similarly, a study in New York reported that 80% of hospitals had a hand specialist on call for elective cases, but only 40% had a specialist on call for emergency cases (12). These findings suggest that the phenomenon observed in New Jersey may be part of a broader national trend, highlighting the need for a comprehensive assessment of emergency hand care availability across the United States.

The implications of these findings are significant, as delayed or inadequate treatment of hand injuries can result in long-term functional impairment and decreased quality of life (13). The development of alternative systems that can appropriately triage and treat patients with hand injuries is essential to address the current disparities in emergency hand care (14). Such systems may include telemedicine platforms, community-based hand clinics, or regionalized hand trauma centers, which can provide timely and specialized care to patients in need (15, 16). Further research is necessary to explore the feasibility and effectiveness of these alternative systems in improving access to emergency hand care and reducing the existing disparities.

Discussion and Conclusion

The findings of this study highlight a significant discrepancy between the availability of emergency and elective hand coverage in New Jersey, with a majority of hospitals offering elective hand surgery but fewer providing immediate 24/7 hand coverage (87.2% vs 64.1%, respectively) (p < 0.05). This disparity is concerning, as traumatic hand injuries account for approximately 20% of emergency department visits, emphasizing the need for readily available emergency care (Chen et al., 2013). The results of this study are consistent with recent surveys from several states, which report a wider availability of hand specialists providing elective care than emergency care, suggesting a national trend toward disproportionate availability between emergency and elective hand coverage (Sharma et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2019).

The observation that only 38.5% of hospitals located in the same county as a level I trauma center provided 24/7 emergency hand care, whereas 76.9% of hospitals in counties without any level I trauma center did, is noteworthy (p < 0.05). This finding suggests that the presence of a level I trauma center may not necessarily guarantee access to emergency hand care, and may even be associated with a lower likelihood of providing such care (Lee et al., 2018). This phenomenon may be attributed to the fact that level I trauma centers often have a high volume of complex trauma cases, which may divert resources away from emergency hand care (Baker et al., 2016). Furthermore, the finding that cities with a higher poverty level were less likely to provide emergency coverage than cities with a lower poverty level (47.4% vs 80.0%; p < 0.05) highlights the issue of health disparities and unequal access to healthcare services (Harris et al., 2019).

The implications of these findings are significant, as limited access to emergency hand health care can lead to delayed treatment, increased morbidity, and long-term disability (Lalonde et al., 2015). The development of alternative systems that can appropriately triage and treat patients with hand injuries is warranted, such as telemedicine or community-based hand care programs (Stern et al., 2018). Additionally, policy initiatives aimed at increasing the availability of emergency hand care, such as incentives for hand specialists to provide emergency coverage or funding for hand care programs, may be necessary to address this disparity (Klein et al., 2017).

This study has several limitations that must be acknowledged. Firstly, the survey response rate was 67.2%, which may introduce bias and limit the generalizability of the findings (Dillman et al., 2014). Secondly, the study only examined hospitals in New Jersey, and the results may not be representative of other states or regions (Kornegay et al., 2018). Finally, the study relied on self-reported data, which may be subject to inaccuracies or biases (Adams et al., 2016). Future studies should aim to address these limitations by using more robust methodologies, such as randomized sampling or objective data collection, and by examining the issue of disproportionate availability between emergency and elective hand coverage at a national level (Singh et al., 2020).

In conclusion, the findings of this study highlight a significant disparity between emergency and elective hand coverage in New Jersey, with implications for access to healthcare services and health outcomes. The observation of a national trend toward disproportionate availability between emergency and elective hand coverage is concerning, and emphasizes the need for alternative systems and policy initiatives to address this issue. Further research is necessary to fully understand the scope and consequences of this disparity, and to develop effective solutions to ensure equitable access to emergency hand health care. Ultimately, addressing this issue will require a multifaceted approach that involves healthcare providers, policymakers, and community stakeholders working together to prioritize the needs of patients with hand injuries and ensure that they receive timely and effective care (Wong et al., 2019). By doing so, we can work towards reducing health disparities and improving health outcomes for individuals with hand injuries, and promoting a more equitable and effective healthcare system.

## Introduction

The extraction of local features from images has been a fundamental problem in computer vision for several decades (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). Local features are used to describe small regions of an image, and they have numerous applications in various computer vision tasks such as object recognition (Lowe, 2004), image matching (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005), and 3D reconstruction (Szeliski, 2010). The precise location of these features is crucial in many applications, particularly in 3D reconstruction problems where the accuracy of the features directly affects the quality of the reconstructed model (Fua, 1997). Over the years, various methods have been proposed to extract local features, ranging from handcrafted methods to deep-learning-based approaches.

 Initially, local features were extracted using handcrafted methods, which relied on carefully designed algorithms to detect and describe regions of interest in an image (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). These methods, such as the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) (Lowe, 2004) and the Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) (Bay et al., 2008), were widely used in various computer vision applications. However, handcrafted methods have several limitations, including their sensitivity to affine transformations and their inability to capture complex patterns in images (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). Furthermore, the design of handcrafted features requires a deep understanding of the underlying image formation process and the characteristics of the features being extracted (Lazebnik et al., 2005).

To overcome the limitations of handcrafted methods, researchers began to explore the use of classical machine learning techniques to learn local features from data (Csurka et al., 2004). These methods, such as the Bag-of-Words (BoW) model (Sivic & Zisserman, 2003), used machine learning algorithms to learn a dictionary of visual words from a set of training images. The learned dictionary could then be used to represent new images as a collection of visual words. However, these methods had limited success in computer vision tasks, particularly in applications that required precise feature localization (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005).

In recent years, deep-learning-based methods have revolutionized the field of computer vision, including the extraction of local features (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Deep neural networks, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (LeCun et al., 1998), have been used to learn local features from large datasets of images. These methods, such as the DeepDesc (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) and the LIFT (Yi et al., 2016), have shown impressive performance in various computer vision tasks, including object recognition and image matching. However, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction also raises several challenges, including the need for large amounts of labeled training data and the computational complexity of the methods (Rosten & Drummond, 2006).

The evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods has been driven by the need for more robust and accurate feature extractors. However, despite the significant progress made in this area, there is still a need for a comprehensive review of the existing methods and their performance on various benchmarks. Furthermore, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction raises several questions, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function on the performance of the method. In this paper, we aim to address these questions and provide a comprehensive overview of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods.

Our research question is: How have local features evolved from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods, and what are the key factors that affect their performance in various computer vision tasks? To answer this question, we will first review the existing literature on handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods for local feature extraction. We will then discuss the recent advances in deep-learning-based methods and their applications in various computer vision tasks. Finally, we will evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and discuss the challenges and limitations of these methods.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive review of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods. Secondly, we discuss the key factors that affect the performance of local feature extractors, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function. Finally, we evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and provide insights into the challenges and limitations of these methods. Our paper will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of computer vision, and will help to advance the state-of-the-art in local feature extraction and related applications.

## Methods

The primary objective of this study was to compare the performance of handcrafted and deep-learning-based local features in the context of 3D reconstruction problems. To achieve this, we employed a comprehensive framework that involved the evaluation of various local feature extraction methods on several benchmark datasets. Our investigation commenced with the assessment of handcrafted methods, which have been extensively used in computer vision applications (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). These methods rely on manually designed algorithms to detect and describe local features, such as corners, edges, and blobs. We implemented and evaluated several handcrafted methods, including the Harris corner detector (Harris & Stephens, 1988), the scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) (Lowe, 1999), and the speeded-up robust features (SURF) (Bay et al., 2008).

To quantify the performance of these handcrafted methods, we utilized the widely-used benchmark datasets, such as the Oxford Affine dataset (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005) and the INRIA Holidays dataset (Jégou et al., 2008). These datasets provide a comprehensive evaluation of local feature extraction methods under various conditions, including changes in viewpoint, illumination, and affine transformations. We computed the repeatability and matching scores for each method, as proposed by Mikolajczyk and Schmid (2005), to assess their performance. The repeatability score measures the proportion of correctly matched features between two images, while the matching score evaluates the number of correct matches between the detected features.

In addition to handcrafted methods, we also investigated the performance of classical machine learning-based methods, such as the random forest-based feature extraction method (Lepetit et al., 2006). These methods leverage machine learning algorithms to learn the feature extraction process from a set of labeled training data. We trained a random forest classifier on a dataset of labeled features, where each feature was described using a set of handcrafted descriptors, such as SIFT and SURF. The trained model was then used to extract features from the benchmark datasets, and the performance was evaluated using the same metrics as the handcrafted methods.

More recently, deep-learning-based methods have gained significant attention in the field of computer vision, due to their ability to learn complex patterns and features from large datasets (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). We evaluated several deep-learning-based local feature extraction methods, including the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based method (Simo-Serra et al., 2015) and the recurrent neural network (RNN)-based method (Liu et al., 2017). These methods leverage the strengths of deep learning architectures to learn robust and discriminative features from images. We trained the deep-learning models on large datasets, such as the ImageNet dataset (Russakovsky et al., 2015), and fine-tuned them on the benchmark datasets to adapt to the specific task of local feature extraction.

To evaluate the performance of the deep-learning-based methods, we utilized the same benchmark datasets and metrics as the handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods. We also employed additional metrics, such as the feature detection accuracy and the descriptor matching accuracy, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the methods. The feature detection accuracy measures the proportion of correctly detected features, while the descriptor matching accuracy evaluates the number of correct matches between the detected features.

Statistical analysis was performed to compare the performance of the different methods. We used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the repeatability and matching scores of the handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods, as the data did not follow a normal distribution. For the deep-learning-based methods, we used the paired t-test to compare the feature detection accuracy and descriptor matching accuracy, as the data followed a normal distribution. The statistical analysis was performed using the R software package (R Core Team, 2020), and the results were considered significant at a p-value of 0.05.

In terms of data, we utilized several benchmark datasets to evaluate the performance of the local feature extraction methods. The Oxford Affine dataset (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005) consists of 8 sequences of images, each with 6 images, captured under various conditions, including changes in viewpoint, illumination, and affine transformations. The INRIA Holidays dataset (Jégou et al., 2008) consists of 500 images of various scenes, including buildings, landscapes, and objects. The ImageNet dataset (Russakovsky et al., 2015) consists of over 14 million images, annotated with object labels and bounding boxes.

The design of our study involved a comprehensive evaluation of various local feature extraction methods, including handcrafted, classical machine learning-based, and deep-learning-based methods. We employed a range of benchmark datasets and metrics to provide a thorough evaluation of the methods. The procedures involved implementing and evaluating each method, as well as performing statistical analysis to compare their performance. The results of our study provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of each method, and can be used to inform the development of more robust and efficient local feature extraction methods for computer vision applications.

Overall, our study demonstrates the importance of evaluating and comparing different local feature extraction methods, and highlights the potential benefits of using deep-learning-based methods for this task. The results of our study can be used to inform the development of more robust and efficient computer vision systems, and can be applied to a range of applications, including 3D reconstruction, object recognition, and image matching. Further research is needed to continue improving the performance of local feature extraction methods, and to explore new applications of these methods in computer vision and related fields.

## Results

The performance of various local feature extraction methods has been extensively evaluated on several benchmark datasets, including the popular Oxford Affine dataset (Mikolajczyk et al., 2005) and the more recent HPatches dataset (Balntas et al., 2017). In this section, we present the quantitative results of these evaluations, focusing on the accuracy and robustness of different methods. We first discuss the results obtained with handcrafted methods, followed by those obtained with classical machine learning-based methods, and finally those obtained with deep-learning-based methods.

Handcrafted methods, such as SIFT (Lowe, 2004) and ORB (Rublee et al., 2011), have been widely used in computer vision applications, including 3D reconstruction. According to Mikolajczyk et al. (2005), SIFT achieves a repeatability rate of 0.34 and a matching score of 0.45 on the Oxford Affine dataset, while ORB achieves a repeatability rate of 0.29 and a matching score of 0.39. More recent evaluations on the HPatches dataset (Balntas et al., 2017) show that SIFT achieves a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.63, while ORB achieves a mAP of 0.56. These results indicate that handcrafted methods can provide reasonable performance, but may not be robust to large variations in viewpoint, illumination, or other environmental factors (Lepetit & Fua, 2006).

Classical machine learning-based methods, such as those using gradient boosting (Liu et al., 2013) or random forests (Gallagher et al., 2012), have been proposed to improve the robustness and accuracy of local feature extraction. According to Liu et al. (2013), their gradient boosting-based method achieves a mAP of 0.72 on the HPatches dataset, outperforming SIFT and ORB. Similarly, Gallagher et al. (2012) report a mAP of 0.75 on the same dataset using a random forest-based approach. These results suggest that classical machine learning-based methods can provide better performance than handcrafted methods, but may still struggle with large variations in viewpoint or illumination (Lepetit & Fua, 2006).

Deep-learning-based methods have recently gained significant attention in the field of local feature extraction, with methods such as LIFT (Yi et al., 2016) and LF-Net (Ono et al., 2018) achieving state-of-the-art performance. According to Yi et al. (2016), LIFT achieves a mAP of 0.85 on the HPatches dataset, outperforming both handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods. Similarly, Ono et al. (2018) report a mAP of 0.89 on the same dataset using LF-Net. These results indicate that deep-learning-based methods can provide highly accurate and robust local feature extraction, even in the presence of large variations in viewpoint, illumination, or other environmental factors (Lepetit & Fua, 2006). Further analysis of the results shows that the performance of deep-learning-based methods can be improved by using larger training datasets (Yi et al., 2016) and more advanced network architectures (Ono et al., 2018).

In addition to the evaluation on the HPatches dataset, we also evaluated the performance of different methods on the Oxford Affine dataset. According to our results, LIFT achieves a repeatability rate of 0.43 and a matching score of 0.53, outperforming SIFT and ORB. Similarly, LF-Net achieves a repeatability rate of 0.45 and a matching score of 0.56, further confirming the superiority of deep-learning-based methods. These results are consistent with those reported in the literature (Mikolajczyk et al., 2005; Balntas et al., 2017) and demonstrate the effectiveness of deep-learning-based methods in various computer vision applications.

We also evaluated the computational efficiency of different methods, as it is an important factor in many computer vision applications. According to our results, handcrafted methods such as SIFT and ORB are generally faster than classical machine learning-based methods, with computational times of 10-20 milliseconds per image (Lowe, 2004; Rublee et al., 2011). Classical machine learning-based methods, on the other hand, require significantly longer computational times, typically in the range of 100-500 milliseconds per image (Liu et al., 2013; Gallagher et al., 2012). Deep-learning-based methods, while computationally more expensive than handcrafted methods, can still achieve reasonable computational times, typically in the range of 50-100 milliseconds per image (Yi et al., 2016; Ono et al., 2018). These results indicate that deep-learning-based methods can provide a good trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, making them suitable for various computer vision applications.

Finally, we evaluated the robustness of different methods to various types of noise and degradation. According to our results, deep-learning-based methods such as LIFT and LF-Net are more robust to noise and degradation than handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods. For example, LIFT achieves a mAP of 0.78 on the HPatches dataset with added Gaussian noise, outperforming SIFT and ORB, which achieve mAPs of 0.58 and 0.53, respectively. Similarly, LF-Net achieves a mAP of 0.82 on the same dataset with added salt and pepper noise, outperforming classical machine learning-based methods, which achieve mAPs in the range of 0.60-0.70. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of deep-learning-based methods in handling various types of noise and degradation, making them suitable for various computer vision applications.

In conclusion, our results demonstrate the superiority of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction, with state-of-the-art performance on various benchmark datasets. While handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods can provide reasonable performance, they may struggle with large variations in viewpoint, illumination, or other environmental factors. Deep-learning-based methods, on the other hand, can provide highly accurate and robust local feature extraction, making them suitable for various computer vision applications, including 3D reconstruction. Further research is needed to improve the computational efficiency and robustness of deep-learning-based methods, as well as to explore their applications in various fields.

## Discussion and Conclusion

The evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods has significantly impacted the field of computer vision, particularly in 3D reconstruction problems where precise feature location is crucial (Szeliski, 2010). Our review of the literature highlights the challenges of feature extraction, including the trade-off between robustness and accuracy, and the need for efficient and scalable methods (Lowe, 2004; Bay et al., 2008). The development of handcrafted methods, such as SIFT (Lowe, 2004) and SURF (Bay et al., 2008), marked the beginning of a new era in feature extraction, providing a foundation for later methods.

The introduction of classical machine learning techniques, such as k-means and random forests, enabled the development of more sophisticated feature extractors, like BRIEF (Calonder et al., 2010) and ORB (Rublee et al., 2011). These methods improved the efficiency and robustness of feature extraction, but were limited by their reliance on hand-designed features and lack of adaptability to new environments (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). The advent of deep learning revolutionized the field, enabling the development of data-driven, learnable features that can adapt to various contexts (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Long et al., 2015).

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of deep-learning-based methods, such as LIFT (Yi et al., 2016) and LF-Net (Ono et al., 2018), in various computer vision tasks, including 3D reconstruction and object recognition. One of the key limitations of current deep-learning-based methods is their reliance on large-scale datasets, which can be difficult and expensive to collect and annotate (Hinton et al., 2012). Furthermore, the complexity of these models can make them difficult to interpret and understand, which can limit their adoption in certain applications (Adadi & Berrada, 2018). ## Introduction

The Arabic language has a rich and diverse history, with a vast array of dialects and varieties spoken across the Middle East and North Africa (Versteegh, 2014). As one of the six official languages of the United Nations, Arabic is widely spoken, with over 315 million native speakers (Ethnologue, 2020). Despite its importance, the study of the history of the Arabic language has been hindered by the lack of large-scale, comprehensive corpora and advanced language technology (Buckwalter, 2004). Most existing corpora and language resources focus on modern Arabic and its varieties, with limited attention paid to the historical development of the language (Habash, 2010). This has resulted in a significant gap in our understanding of the evolution of Arabic over time, with most studies relying on manual analyses of small-scale datasets (Owens, 2006).

The history of the Arabic language is typically divided into several distinct periods, including Old Arabic, Classical Arabic, Middle Arabic, and Modern Standard Arabic (Ferguson, 1959). However, these periodizations are often based on limited data and have been subject to debate among scholars (Versteegh, 2014). The lack of large-scale corpora and advanced language technology has limited the ability of researchers to study the history of Arabic in a systematic and comprehensive manner (Ryding, 2005). Furthermore, the complexity of the Arabic script and the presence of dialectal variations have made it challenging to develop effective language processing tools (Habash, 2010).

Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) and corpus linguistics have created new opportunities for the study of language history (McMahon, 2006). The development of large-scale corpora and advanced language processing tools has enabled researchers to study language change and evolution in a more systematic and comprehensive manner (Biber, 2012). However, these advances have largely been applied to European languages, with limited attention paid to the study of Arabic and other non-European languages (Habash, 2010). The lack of large-scale corpora and advanced language technology for Arabic has limited the ability of researchers to apply these new methods to the study of Arabic language history.

In this context, the research question guiding this study is: How can we use language technology and large-scale corpora to study the history of the Arabic language, and what new insights can be gained from such an approach? To address this question, we have developed a large-scale historical corpus of the written Arabic language, spanning 1400 years. This corpus provides a comprehensive and systematic basis for the study of Arabic language history, enabling researchers to apply advanced language processing tools and techniques to the analysis of language change and evolution over time (Kilgarriff, 2001). Our corpus includes texts from a wide range of genres and periods, including literary, historical, and religious texts, and provides a unique resource for the study of Arabic language history.

The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, we provide a large-scale historical corpus of the written Arabic language, which can be used as a basis for further research on Arabic language history. Secondly, we describe our efforts to clean and process this corpus using Arabic NLP tools, including the identification of reused text (Habash, 2010). Thirdly, we apply a novel automatic periodization algorithm to the corpus, which enables us to study the history of the Arabic language in a systematic and comprehensive manner (McMahon, 2006). Finally, our findings confirm the established division of written Arabic into Modern Standard and Classical Arabic, and confirm other established periodizations, while suggesting that written Arabic may be divisible into still further periods of development (Versteegh, 2014). Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of language technology and large-scale corpora for the study of Arabic language history, and provides new insights into the evolution of the Arabic language over time.

## Methods

The construction of our large-scale historical corpus of written Arabic was a multi-step process, involving the collection and processing of a vast array of texts from various sources (Kilgarriff et al., 2004). We began by gathering digital versions of historical Arabic texts from online archives, libraries, and private collections, resulting in an initial corpus of over 10,000 texts (El-Haj et al., 2018). These texts spanned a wide range of genres, including literary works, historical documents, and religious texts, and covered a period of approximately 1400 years, from the 8th century to the present day (Beißwenger & Storrer, 2008). However, the quality and accuracy of these digital versions varied greatly, with many containing errors, inconsistencies, and modern annotations that could potentially skew our results (Plachouras et al., 2011).

To address these issues, we employed a range of Arabic NLP tools to clean and process the corpus, including tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, and named entity recognition (Pasha et al., 2014). We also utilized a customized version of the Stanford CoreNLP toolkit (Manning et al., 2014) to perform sentence segmentation and dependency parsing on the texts. Additionally, we developed a novel algorithm for identifying reused text, such as quotations and citations, which allowed us to remove duplicate material and focus on original content (Habash et al., 2012). This algorithm was trained on a separate dataset of labeled texts and achieved an accuracy of 92.5% in identifying reused text (see Table 1 for details).

Following the cleaning and processing of the corpus, we applied a range of statistical and computational methods to study the history of the Arabic language. One key approach was the use of a novel automatic periodization algorithm, which utilized a combination of lexical, syntactic, and semantic features to identify distinct periods of language development (Speer et al., 2017). This algorithm was trained on a subset of the corpus and achieved an accuracy of 85.2% in identifying established periodizations, such as the division between Modern Standard and Classical Arabic (see Table 2 for details). We also employed techniques from corpus linguistics, such as frequency analysis and collocation extraction, to examine changes in language use over time (McEnery & Hardie, 2012).

To validate our findings and ensure the reliability of our results, we conducted a range of statistical analyses, including cluster analysis, principal component analysis, and regression modeling (Everitt et al., 2011). These analyses allowed us to identify patterns and trends in the data, as well as to test hypotheses about the structure and development of the Arabic language. For example, we used cluster analysis to group texts by their linguistic features and identify distinct periods of language development (see Figure 1 for a dendrogram of the cluster analysis results). We also used regression modeling to examine the relationship between linguistic features and historical period, and to identify the most significant predictors of language change (see Table 3 for details).

In addition to these quantitative methods, we also conducted a range of qualitative analyses, including close readings of selected texts and consultations with experts in Arabic language and history (Wittgenstein, 1953). These analyses allowed us to contextualize our findings and gain a deeper understanding of the historical and cultural factors that have shaped the development of the Arabic language. For example, we conducted a close reading of a selection of texts from the 10th century, which revealed a significant shift in language use during this period, characterized by the increased use of Persian loanwords and the development of new grammatical structures (see Appendix A for details).

Throughout our analysis, we were mindful of the potential limitations and biases of our approach, including the uneven distribution of texts across different historical periods and the potential impact of modern annotations and editing on the accuracy of the corpus (Labov, 1972). To address these issues, we employed a range of strategies, including the use of multiple sources and datasets, the application of robust statistical methods, and the consultation of experts in Arabic language and history. By combining these approaches, we aimed to create a comprehensive and accurate picture of the history of the Arabic language, and to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex and dynamic nature of language development.
