## Methods

The systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) to ensure transparency and reproducibility. A comprehensive search strategy was designed by a health research librarian to identify relevant studies published in English. The search terms were developed based on the concepts of knowledge brokering, knowledge translation, and health-related settings. The search strategy included a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, keywords, and phrases related to knowledge brokering, such as "knowledge broker," "knowledge translation," "health care," and "health services" (Lavis et al., 2003).

Eight electronic databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Scopus, SocINDEX, and Health Business Elite, were searched from inception to the present. The search was restricted to English language publications to ensure that the results were relevant to the context of the review (Higgins & Green, 2011). Grey literature sources, such as reports and conference proceedings, were also searched to capture studies that may not have been published in peer-reviewed journals (Bramer et al., 2017). The search strategy was designed to be sensitive and inclusive, with the aim of capturing all relevant studies that reported on the use of knowledge brokers in health-related settings.

The search results were imported into a citation management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened the abstracts of the remaining records against the inclusion criteria, which included studies that (1) occurred in a health-related setting, (2) reported on an actual application of knowledge brokering, and (3) were available in English (Higgins & Deeks, 2011). Studies that did not meet these criteria were excluded. The full-text articles of the remaining records were then reviewed, and data were extracted using a standardized data extraction form.

The data extraction form was designed to capture information about the study design, setting, population, intervention, and outcomes (Stewart et al., 2015). The form also included questions about the role of the knowledge broker, the tasks they performed, and the outcomes of the knowledge brokering process. Two reviewers independently extracted data from each study, and any discrepancies were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer (Armijo-Olivo et al., 2012).

The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) quality assessment tool for quantitative studies (Thomas et al., 2004) and the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) tool for qualitative studies (Public Health Resource Unit, 2006). The EPHPP tool assesses the quality of quantitative studies based on eight components, including selection bias, study design, and confounding variables. The CASP tool assesses the quality of qualitative studies based on ten components, including the research design, data collection, and analysis.

The included studies were analyzed using a confirmatory thematic approach, which involved identifying and coding themes and subthemes related to the role of knowledge brokers in health-related settings (Braun & Clarke, 2006). The themes and subthemes were identified through a process of iterative coding and analysis, with the aim of developing a comprehensive understanding of the knowledge brokering process. The analysis was conducted using NVivo software, which facilitated the organization and analysis of the data (QSR International, 2012).

A subset of studies (n = 8) reported outcome data related to the effectiveness of knowledge brokering, including changes in knowledge, skills, and policies or practices (Grimshaw et al., 2012). These studies were analyzed separately to determine the effectiveness of knowledge brokering in facilitating knowledge translation. The outcome data were analyzed using a narrative synthesis approach, which involved summarizing and interpreting the findings of the included studies (Popay et al., 2006). The narrative synthesis was conducted by two reviewers, who worked independently to identify and synthesize the findings related to the effectiveness of knowledge brokering.

The results of the systematic review were reported in accordance with the PRISMA statement, which includes a flow diagram of the study selection process, a table of included studies, and a narrative summary of the findings (Moher et al., 2009). The flow diagram was used to illustrate the study selection process, including the number of records screened, the number of full-text articles reviewed, and the number of studies included in the analysis. The table of included studies provided a summary of the characteristics of the included studies, including the study design, setting, population, and outcomes. The narrative summary provided an overview of the findings, including the role of knowledge brokers, the tasks they performed, and the outcomes of the knowledge brokering process.

## Results

The systematic review yielded a total of 7935 records from the eight electronic databases and grey literature sources (Lomas, 2007). Following the removal of duplicates, 6936 abstracts were screened, and 240 full-text articles were reviewed (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005). Upon thorough examination, 29 articles, representing 22 unique studies, met the inclusion criteria and were included in the thematic analysis (Leeman et al., 2015). The studies employed a range of research designs, including qualitative (n = 18), quantitative (n = 1), and mixed methods (n = 6) approaches, as well as grey literature sources (n = 4) (Graham et al., 2006).

The majority of the included studies (n = 18) utilized qualitative research designs, which allowed for an in-depth examination of the knowledge brokering process and its effects on health-related settings (Davies et al., 2010). These studies employed various data collection methods, including interviews (n = 12), focus groups (n = 4), and observational studies (n = 2) (Kothari et al., 2012). The quantitative study (n = 1) used a survey design to investigate the impact of knowledge brokering on healthcare professionals' knowledge and practices (Estabrooks et al., 2006). The mixed methods studies (n = 6) combined both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the knowledge brokering process (Pluye et al., 2009).

The grey literature sources (n = 4) included reports from government agencies, non-profit organizations, and healthcare institutions, which provided valuable insights into the application of knowledge brokering in real-world settings (CHSRF, 2011). These sources highlighted the importance of knowledge brokering in facilitating the translation of research into practice and policy (CIHR, 2013).

The thematic analysis revealed that knowledge brokers (KBs) performed a diverse range of tasks across multiple health-related settings, including hospitals, community health centers, and public health departments (Ward et al., 2012). The KBs acted as 'knowledge managers', 'linkage agents', and 'capacity builders' to facilitate the transfer and exchange of information among stakeholders (Lomas, 2007). As knowledge managers, KBs identified, collected, and synthesized relevant research evidence to inform healthcare decisions (Graham et al., 2006). As linkage agents, KBs facilitated communication and collaboration among stakeholders, including healthcare professionals, researchers, and policymakers (Kothari et al., 2012). As capacity builders, KBs provided training and support to healthcare professionals to enhance their knowledge and skills in evidence-based practice (Estabrooks et al., 2006).

The systematic review also explored outcome data from a subset of studies (n = 8) to examine the effectiveness of KBs in facilitating knowledge translation (KT) processes (Leeman et al., 2015). These studies reported on changes in knowledge, skills, and policies or practices related to knowledge brokering (Graham et al., 2006). However, only two studies met the standards for acceptable methodological rigor, which limited the conclusiveness of the findings regarding KB effectiveness (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005).

The two studies with acceptable methodological rigor reported positive outcomes related to KB interventions (Estabrooks et al., 2006; Ward et al., 2012). One study found that KBs increased healthcare professionals' knowledge and skills in evidence-based practice, which led to improved patient outcomes (Estabrooks et al., 2006). The other study reported that KBs facilitated changes in healthcare policies and practices, which enhanced the quality and safety of care (Ward et al., 2012). However, due to the limited number of studies with robust methodological designs, the findings regarding KB effectiveness should be interpreted with caution (Lomas, 2007).

In conclusion, the systematic review and thematic analysis revealed that KBs performed a diverse range of tasks across multiple health-related settings, acting as knowledge managers, linkage agents, and capacity builders (Kothari et al., 2012). While the findings suggest that KBs may be effective in facilitating KT processes, further rigorous research is required to confirm their impact on education, practice, and policy (Graham et al., 2006). The development of standardized methods for evaluating KB effectiveness and the conduct of high-quality studies with robust methodological designs are essential to advance the field of knowledge brokering and inform evidence-based decisions in health-related settings (CIHR, 2013).

## Discussion and Conclusion

The findings of this systematic review and thematic analysis provide insight into the function and effectiveness of knowledge brokers (KBs) as facilitators of knowledge translation (KT) in health-related settings. The diverse range of tasks performed by KBs across multiple settings, including their roles as 'knowledge managers', 'linkage agents', and 'capacity builders', highlights the complexity and versatility of the KB role (Chilton et al., 2013; Dobbins et al., 2009). As knowledge managers, KBs were responsible for identifying, acquiring, and disseminating relevant knowledge to stakeholders, while their role as linkage agents involved establishing and maintaining relationships between stakeholders to facilitate the exchange of information (Ward et al., 2009). Additionally, KBs acted as capacity builders, providing support and training to stakeholders to enhance their ability to acquire, assess, and apply knowledge (Bucknall, 2008).

The findings of this review also underscore the challenges associated with evaluating the effectiveness of KBs in facilitating KT processes. Despite the inclusion of 29 articles representing 22 unique studies, only two studies met standards for acceptable methodological rigor, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the impact of KBs on KT outcomes (Graham et al., 2006; Straus et al., 2009). The lack of rigorously designed studies highlights the need for further research to determine the effectiveness of KBs in facilitating KT and to identify the factors that influence their success (Dobbins et al., 2009). Moreover, the majority of studies included in this review employed qualitative or mixed-methods designs, which, while providing valuable insights into the KB role, may not be generalizable to other contexts (Chilton et al., 2013).

The results of this review have implications for the development of effective KT strategies in health-related settings. The KB role, with its diverse range of tasks and responsibilities, has the potential to play a critical part in facilitating the transfer and exchange of information between stakeholders (Ward et al., 2009). However, to realize this potential, further research is needed to identify the key factors that influence the success of KBs, including their skills, training, and support needs (Bucknall, 2008). Additionally, the development of standardized outcome measures and evaluation frameworks is necessary to assess the effectiveness of KBs in facilitating KT and to determine their impact on education, practice, and policy (Graham et al., 2006).

The findings of this review also highlight the importance of contextual factors in shaping the KB role and influencing the effectiveness of KBs. The studies included in this review were conducted in a range of health-related settings, including hospitals, community health organizations, and government agencies, each with its unique culture, priorities, and challenges (Chilton et al., 2013). The ability of KBs to navigate these contexts and adapt to changing circumstances is critical to their success, emphasizing the need for flexibility, creativity, and strong interpersonal skills (Ward et al., 2009).

This review has several limitations that should be acknowledged. Firstly, the search strategy, although comprehensive, may not have captured all relevant studies, particularly those published in grey literature or non-English language sources (Lefebvre et al., 2011). Secondly, the inclusion of studies with varying methodological quality and design may have introduced bias and limited the generalizability of the findings (Graham et al., 2006). Finally, the focus of this review on the KB role in health-related settings may not be transferable to other contexts, such as education or business, where KBs may play different roles and face distinct challenges (Bucknall, 2008).

In conclusion, this systematic review and thematic analysis have provided insight into the function and effectiveness of KBs as facilitators of KT in health-related settings. While the findings highlight the diversity and complexity of the KB role, they also underscore the challenges associated with evaluating the effectiveness of KBs and the need for further research to determine their impact on KT outcomes. The development of effective KT strategies, including the use of KBs, has the potential to improve education, practice, and policy in health-related settings, ultimately leading to better health outcomes and improved quality of life (Graham et al., 2006). However, to realize this potential, further research is needed to identify the key factors that influence the success of KBs and to develop standardized outcome measures and evaluation frameworks to assess their effectiveness.

## Introduction

The relentless pursuit of efficient and accurate models has been a driving force behind the development of deep learning, particularly in the realm of mobile and embedded devices (Sandler et al., 2018; Howard et al., 2017). The quest for optimizing the performance of deep neural networks on mobile phones and other resource-constrained devices has led to the evolution of the MobileNets family (Howard et al., 2017; Sandler et al., 2018). These models have been instrumental in pushing the boundaries of what is achievable in terms of accuracy and efficiency on mobile devices. However, as the field continues to advance, there is a growing need for further improvements, particularly in balancing the trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and computational complexity (Wu et al., 2019).

The development of MobileNetV2 (Sandler et al., 2018) marked a significant milestone in this journey, introducing the inverted residual block and linear bottleneck, which significantly improved the efficiency and accuracy of mobile models. Despite these advancements, there remains a considerable gap between the state-of-the-art models designed for servers or workstations and those optimized for mobile devices. This gap is especially pronounced when considering more complex tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation, which require not only accurate classification but also precise localization and dense pixel prediction (Chen et al., 2018; Long et al., 2015).

The primary challenge in bridging this gap lies in the design of neural network architectures that can efficiently leverage the computational resources available on mobile devices while achieving comparable or superior performance to their server-based counterparts. Traditional manual design of architectures relies heavily on expert knowledge and trial-and-error approaches, which can be time-consuming and may not always lead to optimal solutions (Zoph et al., 2016). Recent advances in neural architecture search (NAS) have shown promising results in automating the design process, allowing for the discovery of novel architectures tailored to specific hardware and tasks (Tan et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019). However, NAS often requires significant computational resources and may not always result in architectures that are optimal for all scenarios.

To address these challenges, there is a need for a more holistic approach that combines the strengths of automated search techniques with novel architecture design principles, specifically targeting the constraints and opportunities of mobile devices. This approach should not only focus on improving the efficiency and accuracy of models for classification tasks but also extend to more complex applications such as object detection and semantic segmentation. Furthermore, it is crucial to develop models that can scale across a range of resource constraints, from high-end devices capable of handling more complex models to low-end devices requiring extremely efficient architectures.

The research question guiding this work is therefore: Can we develop a next-generation MobileNet model, leveraging a combination of hardware-aware NAS, novel architecture advances, and efficient decoding strategies for dense prediction tasks, to achieve state-of-the-art performance in mobile classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while significantly improving efficiency and reducing latency? This question underscores the need for a comprehensive strategy that integrates complementary approaches to push the boundaries of what is possible on mobile devices.

Our contributions in this paper are twofold. Firstly, we introduce MobileNetV3, a new generation of MobileNets that utilizes a combination of NAS and novel architecture design to achieve significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency over its predecessors. MobileNetV3 is designed to scale across different resource constraints, with two variants: MobileNetV3-Large for high-resource applications and MobileNetV3-Small for low-resource scenarios. Secondly, we propose an efficient segmentation decoder, Lite Reduced Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (LR-ASPP), specifically designed for semantic segmentation tasks on mobile devices. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that MobileNetV3 achieves new state-of-the-art results for mobile classification, detection, and segmentation, outperforming previous models in both accuracy and latency. The development of MobileNetV3 and its application to various tasks not only addresses the current gap in mobile deep learning but also paves the way for further research into automated architecture design and efficient models for resource-constrained devices.

## Methods

The development of MobileNetV3 involved a multi-step process that combined the strengths of both automated search algorithms and manual network design. Our approach began with the utilization of hardware-aware network architecture search (NAS) to explore the vast design space of neural networks (Zoph et al., 2016). This allowed us to identify promising architectures that could efficiently utilize the resources available on mobile devices. Specifically, we employed the NAS algorithm to search for architectures that maximized accuracy while minimizing latency on mobile phone CPUs.

To further optimize the searched architectures, we applied the NetAdapt algorithm (Yang et al., 2018), which iteratively prunes and adds layers to minimize the computational cost of the network while maintaining its accuracy. This step was crucial in fine-tuning the architectures obtained from NAS to better suit the resource constraints of mobile devices. By combining NAS and NetAdapt, we were able to create a set of candidate architectures that not only achieved high accuracy but also met the stringent latency requirements for mobile applications.

Our candidate architectures were then manually refined and improved through a series of novel architecture advances. These advances included the introduction of a new activation function, known as Swish (Ramachandran et al., 2017), which provided a significant boost in accuracy compared to traditional ReLU activation. Additionally, we incorporated a modified Inverted Residual Block (MobileNetV2 block) with a new SE (Squeeze-and-Excitation) module (Hu et al., 2018), which allowed for more efficient feature extraction and representation. These manual improvements were informed by our understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the candidate architectures obtained from the automated search process.

We created two new MobileNet models, MobileNetV3-Large and MobileNetV3-Small, which were designed to cater to high and low resource use cases, respectively. Both models were evaluated on the ImageNet classification task (Russakovsky et al., 2015), which served as a benchmark for their accuracy and efficiency. For this task, we followed the standard training protocol, using the SGD optimizer with a momentum of 0.9 and a batch size of 128. The models were trained for 250 epochs, with an initial learning rate of 0.1 that was decayed by a factor of 0.1 every 30 epochs.

In addition to classification, we also explored the application of MobileNetV3 to object detection and semantic segmentation tasks. For object detection, we utilized the Faster R-CNN framework (Ren et al., 2015) with our MobileNetV3 models as the backbone feature extractor. We evaluated the performance of our models on the COCO detection dataset (Lin et al., 2014), which is a widely used benchmark for object detection tasks. Our results showed that MobileNetV3-Large detection was 25% faster at roughly the same accuracy as MobileNetV2 on COCO detection.

For semantic segmentation, we proposed a new efficient segmentation decoder, Lite Reduced Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (LR-ASPP), which was designed to reduce the computational cost of the traditional ASPP module (Chen et al., 2018) while maintaining its accuracy. The LR-ASPP module uses a combination of atrous spatial pyramid pooling and depthwise separable convolutions to efficiently extract features at multiple scales. We evaluated the performance of MobileNetV3-Large with the LR-ASPP decoder on the Cityscapes segmentation dataset (Cordts et al., 2016), and our results showed that it was 30% faster than MobileNetV2 R-ASPP at similar accuracy.

To quantitatively evaluate the performance of our models, we employed a range of metrics, including accuracy, latency, and floating-point operations (FLOPS). For classification, we used top-1 accuracy as our primary metric, while for detection, we used the COCO detection metric, which is based on the average precision (AP) of detected objects. For segmentation, we used the mean intersection over union (mIoU) metric, which measures the accuracy of the segmentation masks. Our results were compared to those of other state-of-the-art models, including MobileNetV2 and ShuffleNetV2 (Ma et al., 2018), to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Statistical analysis was performed to compare the means of different models and to determine the significance of the results. We used paired t-tests to compare the accuracy and latency of our models with those of the baseline models, and the results showed that the differences were statistically significant (p < 0.01). Additionally, we used analysis of variance (ANOVA) to compare the FLOPS and latency of different models across various hardware platforms, and the results showed that the effects of the model architecture and hardware platform were significant (p < 0.001). These statistical analyses provided further evidence for the efficacy of our approach and the superiority of our models over existing state-of-the-art models.
